The articles backtracked from their original incendiary, and now clearly false, claims to something more like "Jensen did lawful things that powerful people didn't like". It still appears the original claims came from a single competing Big Tech lobbyist.

The reporting successfully disrupted corporate governance processes, with a running cost of $1.8 trillion in losses to American pension funds and shareholders.

Here's what I fear is being lost in these articles: The proper interface between government and private citizens and their corporations is rule of law. Laws are passed, and if wrongdoing as alleged, then there's due process: an investigation followed by facts and evidence presented in open court. Due process should happen here: let the facts come out whole, and not as a trickle of dubious claims.

Press takedowns full of sketchily sourced claims and backtracking narratives are not the way. It's what we see outside of the free world, and is no model for The United States of America.

In particular, if the Jensen takedown succeeds on the basis of these journalistic failings, which is not by any means certain as Sam Altman's case shows, then it foreshadows an economically and institutionally ruinous new playbook to be adopted with no end in sight.

Imagine a weekly stream of takedowns emerging from opportunistic alignments between corporate lobbyists and political interests which, given the new partisan split between the executive and legislative branches, will attack in all directions, undermining not only the US economy but American leadership in the world.

I hope cooler heads prevail this coming week as they did not on Thursday November 12. And I urge anyone who happened to oppose Jensen, open models, and the underlying trade policies in question, to recognize that this isn't a win for "team regulation". It's a change in the game from a transparent rules-based one to a sinister new form centered around politicans and lobbyists.

text:
I'm a social media manager at the White House, where I draft posts for the President's Truth Social account. I have some insider information regarding the FAA ground stop, specifically whose fault it was.

The writing takes 10 minutes. The real work is attribution. When something breaks, I decide which president broke it. On Sunday I assigned Friday’s ground stop to Joe Biden.

In the building we don’t say blame. We say custody. A failure is a hot potato, and it never stops moving. On Friday the Secretary of Transportation handed it to the old routers. On Saturday he handed it to the contractor. The contractor announced its fiber conversion was more than 70% complete, which handed it back to the FAA. The FAA Administrator called Friday’s work routine maintenance, which handed it back to the Secretary. The potato went around the building twice and came back hot. My job is to stop the music while it’s in the hands of someone who has left town.

It took 4 days. The press says the President spent them out of public view. He didn’t. He spent the weekend on Truth Social, posting photos of a golf course. We spent it at the whiteboard.

The whiteboard in our office has every president since 2002 in a different marker color. Bush is green. Obama is blue. Biden is red, and red is the only marker we keep stocked.

Here was the problem. On Friday a router flooded the FAA’s network and grounded the country. A contractor was swapping copper wire for fiber at a remote site. The contractor is L3Harris. Its predecessor, Harris Corp., won the contract in July 2002. That’s George W. Bush. CBS sources said the routers involved were built between 2001 and 2006. That’s also Bush.

Bush doesn’t post. You can’t blame a man who paints dogs.

So I went through the folders. In 2009 a Harris technician misconfigured a router while moving the network to fiber, disrupting 129 facilities. That’s Obama. But Obama was 2 presidents ago, and the base doesn’t remember 2009. In September 2017 the FAA published a paper warning that its telecommunications were aging and that most operational services ran on old TDM links. 2017 is a problem year.

On Saturday night an intern found the 2017 paper and asked who was president that year. Nobody answered. We moved to the next slide. The intern now works on the Thanksgiving folder.
The President came by the Saturday meeting once. He looked at the whiteboard for a long time. He said 3 words: “Old broken stuff.” Then he left. Nobody knew whether he meant the routers or the whiteboard. We put both in the post.

Then I found 2023. In March 2023 the FAA gave Verizon a contract worth up to $2.4 billion to replace the old network. That’s Biden. In September 2024 the Government Accountability Office reported that 105 of the FAA’s 138 air traffic control systems were unsustainable or potentially unsustainable. Also Biden. I had my president.

I left out 2 dates. In August 2026 we moved the replacement network from Verizon to AT&T. Verizon is a Biden vendor now. AT&T is ours until something breaks. In September 2026 the GAO found the FAA’s modernization had no comprehensive life cycle cost estimate and no integrated schedule. Both happened on our watch. Neither one fit in the post.

The post went through 4 drafts.

Draft 1 blamed L3Harris. Legal reminded me that L3Harris makes radios for the Pentagon. You don’t blame a defense contractor you’ll need for the next war.
Draft 2 blamed the router. Routers don’t have a party. The post tested flat.
Draft 3 blamed AI. The FAA cleared AI on Saturday morning. Someone from the AI office called within the hour.
Draft 4 blamed Biden. It went out at 9 a.m. Sunday.

Here’s the published version: “The Biden administration was an FAA disaster. Everything they touched turned bad. Big money spent unwisely, making an old and broken system worse than when they began.” I’m proud of “when they began.” The system they began with was the one Harris started building in 2002. Biden made it worse. Bush made it.

Then the ask: “We have the knowledge and plan for the flight control systems; we need Congress to give the money, fast!” The GAO reviewed the modernization plan in September. It found no cost estimate and no schedule. Our plan has knowledge. It just doesn’t have dates or prices yet. That’s what the money is for.
The same post says, “Our FAA is doing a great job, and is ready to go.” On Friday the FAA was not ready to go. Nobody was ready to go. That was the point of the ground stop.

The second post went further. The President wrote that much of the system was 50 years old and called it “RIDICULOUS.” That word left my desk in lowercase. It came back in capitals. I never ask who does the capitals.

Then: “We have already started the work, but it should be done all at once, not in drips and drabs.” I don’t know what a drab is. Nobody on staff does. It’s federal policy now. As for the drips, Congress gave the FAA $12.5 billion in July 2025. The President asked for about $30 billion more. On Friday night the Secretary asked for $50 billion. The ask grew by $20 billion in one evening. Somebody left the faucet running. The administration still hasn’t published a full breakdown of how it would spend the $50 billion.
The post ends, “The Biden Administration set it back years!” I counted. The network is 24 years old. Biden had it for 4.

I had a second assignment this weekend: the President’s golf course. In October we posted that the East Potomac Golf Course would close “as scheduled on November 15th” for “Competitive (with other such projects!), Safety, Modernization, and Aesthetic reasons.” Both of my projects this weekend were modernizations. Only the golf course had a schedule.

On Saturday a federal judge blocked the closure for 2 weeks. She cited our posts. Judge Ana Reyes wrote that they “indicate that the Washington National Plan is final.” Nobody had ever called one of our plans final. The first person to do it was a judge, and she meant it as evidence.
The President wrote that the judge “doesn’t want us to quickly and inexpensively fix up the Course which is, also, very dangerous.” The Secretary says the airspace is “a safe system.” So here is the administration’s position. The golf course is very dangerous and needs a quick, inexpensive fix. The airspace is safe and needs $50 billion, all at once.

We have a punctuation rulebook. Each post gets 1 exclamation point. The first FAA post spent it on “fast!” The second spent it on “set it back years!” Golf is exempt. “They don’t call it Trash Island for no reason!”
The engineers made my job harder. On Saturday the FAA Administrator said Friday’s router swap was routine maintenance, not part of the modernization. Routine maintenance happens on the current president’s watch. I can’t send routine maintenance to Delaware. So the post doesn’t mention the router. It mentions “an old and broken system.” Old is always someone else’s.

L3Harris says its conversion is more than 70% complete. That’s useful too. If it finishes, it was our plan. If it breaks, it was 70% Biden.

The President had reportedly said those same 3 words, “old broken stuff,” to Peter Doocy on Friday. That’s still the best root-cause analysis this building has produced. It names no vendor, no year and no president. I’m saving it for the next outage.

Our blame policy fits on one line of the whiteboard. Every failure belongs to the most recent president who can’t hold a press conference about it. Bush is retired. Obama is too far back for the base. Biden is perfect. He’s recent enough to blame and gone enough not to answer. Above my desk there’s a sign, like the ones in factories: DAYS SINCE LAST PREDECESSOR: 0.

Tonight I started a folder called “Thanksgiving delays.” It’s empty, except for a sticky note with the first word. The marker is red.

author: BillAckman
quoted_text:
The articles backtracked from their original incendiary, and now clearly false, claims to something more like "Jensen did lawful things that powerful people didn't like". It still appears the original claims came from a single competing Big Tech lobbyist.

The reporting successfully disrupted corporate governance processes, with a running cost of $1.8 trillion in losses to American pension funds and shareholders.

Here's what I fear is being lost in these articles: The proper interface between government and private citizens and their corporations is rule of law. Laws are passed, and if wrongdoing as alleged, then there's due process: an investigation followed by facts and evidence presented in open court. Due process should happen here: let the facts come out whole, and not as a trickle of dubious claims.

Press takedowns full of sketchily sourced claims and backtracking narratives are not the way. It's what we see outside of the free world, and is no model for The United States of America.

In particular, if the Jensen takedown succeeds on the basis of these journalistic failings, which is not by any means certain as Sam Altman's case shows, then it foreshadows an economically and institutionally ruinous new playbook to be adopted with no end in sight.

Imagine a weekly stream of takedowns emerging from opportunistic alignments between corporate lobbyists and political interests which, given the new partisan split between the executive and legislative branches, will attack in all directions, undermining not only the US economy but American leadership in the world.

I hope cooler heads prevail this coming week as they did not on Thursday November 12. And I urge anyone who happened to oppose Jensen, open models, and the underlying trade policies in question, to recognize that this isn't a win for "team regulation". It's a change in the game from a transparent rules-based one to a sinister new form centered around politicans and lobbyists.

text:
Looking back at my high school and college class, the people who ended up the most successful was not a surprise at all

Every single person in this category showed signs they would end up doing well pretty early in their life

> maniacal ability to focus on something
> sense of urgency in getting things done
> confidence and self belief
> ability to crowd out noise from external events in their life

Ironically, most of the extremely successful people came from relatively humble backgrounds. 

The folks with rich parents ended up doing well, but not as well as you would have expected. Many of them decided that they were happy with what they have already achieved and stopped pursuing more career success 

Not exactly sure how to describe it, but everyone who ended up very wealthy always had a sense of a chip on their shoulder. Just from speaking with them, you could tell their mission was to prove something about themselves to the world

Many of them had a lot of unfortunate events in their life along the way. Illness of family members, parents passing away at an early age etc. and they still managed to move forward with their career goals despite that

By definition, most of the successful folks were not valedictorians and some didn’t even have top grades in school. However, their personality was the telltale sign that it was going to work out for them. These people knew how to persevere better than anyone else

quoted_text:
Have you ever wondered why catching Starship is so much harder than catching Super Heavy, even though they both return to the same launch tower? 🔥

💡 The answer comes down to four major engineering challenges that make Starship’s recovery fundamentally different 👇

⚡ The first problem is shedding an enormous amount of energy

At hot staging, Super Heavy was traveling at roughly 5,800 km/h (3,600 mph). Starship, meanwhile, had to return from orbital speeds of roughly 27,500 km/h (17,100 mph).

That’s nearly five times faster. Because kinetic energy increases with the square of velocity, each kilogram of Starship at orbital speed carries roughly 22 times the kinetic energy of a kilogram of Super Heavy at separation.

That works out to nearly 30 million joules per kilogram.

Almost all of that energy has to be dissipated before Starship can safely reach the tower.

One option would be to use rocket propulsion to cancel out its orbital velocity. However, scrubbing off roughly 7.7 km/s of speed using Raptor engines alone would require a massive amount of propellant.

The rocket equation makes this approach especially punishing. Every extra kilogram of landing propellant has to be hauled into orbit first, dramatically increasing the fuel needed at liftoff.

Instead, SpaceX uses Earth’s atmosphere to bleed off almost all of Starship’s orbital velocity.

That saves an extraordinary amount of propellant, though it introduces another major hurdle.

🔥 Surviving extreme atmospheric heating comes next

As Starship plunges into the atmosphere at hypersonic speeds, powerful shock waves compress and heat the surrounding air to blistering temperatures.

Thousands of ceramic heat-shield tiles protect its stainless-steel structure from the intense heat.

Simply keeping those tiles attached isn’t enough, though. Superheated gas can seep into the gaps between them, risking damage to the underlying structure.

For Flight 15, SpaceX carried forward upgrades from Flight 14, including extra tile-retention hardware in vulnerable areas and redesigned curved tiles that reduce heating between adjacent tiles.

Because Super Heavy never reaches orbital velocity, its return doesn’t expose it to anything close to the same thermal stress.

And there’s another complication.

A heat shield that survives one reentry isn’t necessarily ready to fly again. Starship’s thermal protection system must eventually withstand repeated missions without major repairs or refurbishment.

That’s critical, since rapid reusability is one of the core reasons SpaceX designed Starship to be caught rather than discarded.

Yet surviving reentry still isn’t enough. Starship also has to arrive at the exact right spot.

🎯 Hitting a precise target from orbit raises the stakes even further

About 56 minutes before the catch, a single Raptor engine fired for just 10 seconds to initiate Starship’s return.

That brief deorbit burn wasn’t meant to eliminate orbital velocity. Instead, it nudged the spacecraft’s trajectory so atmospheric drag could take over the much larger job of slowing it down.

Starship then entered the upper atmosphere thousands of kilometers away over the Pacific Ocean.

From there, its four aerodynamic flaps controlled its orientation and fine-tuned the forces acting on the vehicle.

Super Heavy uses grid fins to steer during its return, but Starship’s flaps have to handle a far wider range of flight conditions.

As Starship decelerates from hypersonic through supersonic and down to subsonic speeds, its guidance system continuously adjusts its attitude and flight path.

The challenge is maintaining the right balance of altitude, speed, and trajectory while aerodynamic forces shift dramatically throughout reentry.

For Flight 15, the return corridor crossed sparsely populated parts of northern Mexico and South Texas.

Starship maneuvered around major population centers in the Rio Grande Valley, passed north of South Padre Island, headed offshore over the Gulf of Mexico, and made its final turn toward Pad 2 at Starbase.

Think about the guidance precision required.

A spacecraft returning from orbit must dissipate nearly all of its immense kinetic energy while threading a carefully controlled trajectory straight back to a single launch tower.

It also has to arrive at a low enough speed, in the proper orientation, and with enough propellant remaining to pull off the final maneuver.

That brings us to the most visually spectacular part of the entire recovery.

🚀 Executing the landing flip with pinpoint precision is the final test

Super Heavy approaches the launch tower already vertical, using its grid fins and Raptor engines to guide its final descent.

Starship comes in belly-first.

It has to rapidly swing its massive frame upright, stabilize its attitude, and align itself precisely between the tower’s mechanical arms.

SpaceX’s official Flight 15 timeline allotted just 18 seconds between the start of Starship’s landing burn and the catch.

During those 18 seconds, three sea-level Raptor engines ignite to kick off the maneuver.

The spacecraft rotates upright while its flight computers constantly regulate engine thrust and vehicle attitude.

The engines then step down from three to two, giving the vehicle finer control as it nears the chopsticks.

Finally, it transitions to a single engine for the last moments of descent before shutting down as the tower takes its weight.

Consider the coordination involved.

The guidance system must balance translation, rotation, thrust, and descent rate while positioning a massive spacecraft within a narrow capture envelope.

Unlike a conventional vertical rocket landing, Starship must first transition from an aerodynamically controlled, belly-first glide to an engine-powered vertical approach.

All of this unfolds within seconds, right after the vehicle has completed one of the most punishing atmospheric reentries ever attempted by a reusable spacecraft.

🧠 What makes SpaceX’s approach so ingenious is how seamlessly the entire recovery system works together

Trying to solve every phase of the return with rocket propulsion would carry a crushing propellant penalty.

Instead, SpaceX delegates the toughest parts of the recovery to systems purpose-built to handle them.

The atmosphere dissipates most of the orbital kinetic energy without consuming onboard propellant.

The heat shield protects Starship from the intense thermal loads of that deceleration.

The four aerodynamic flaps provide the control authority needed to manage its attitude, energy, and trajectory throughout atmospheric flight.

And the Raptor engines take over once aerodynamic control alone can no longer deliver the precision needed for the final catch.

That division of labor allows SpaceX to recover an orbital spacecraft without carrying enough fuel for an all-propulsive return.

Yet the engineering trade-off goes deeper than saving propellant.

SpaceX is shifting much of the cost of returning from orbit away from expendable propellant and toward reusable hardware built to endure extreme thermal and mechanical stress.

The potential economic payoff is enormous.

Cutting back on the propellant reserved for recovery frees up more of Starship’s mass capacity for useful payload. However, that advantage only becomes truly meaningful if the heat shield, flaps, engines, and other systems can survive repeated flights without extensive refurbishment.

That’s why catching Ship 42 is such a landmark milestone.

SpaceX has proven that its thermal protection, aerodynamic controls, propulsion, and guidance systems can work in concert to recover an orbital upper stage right at the launch site.

The next engineering hurdle is proving that the same spacecraft can do it repeatedly.

If SpaceX can bring Starship home, inspect it, refuel it, and launch it again without rebuilding major systems, the economics of getting payload to orbit could change dramatically.

That first catch proves the recovery architecture works. Repeated reflights will determine just how much of its economic potential SpaceX can unlock.

text:
I ran a PageRank-driven analysis on all recent news coverage related to Jensen, and traced how the New York Times shaped the entirety of this narrative: https://t.co/qKGMJ2LBV8

--
NVIDIA has lost over $1 trillion in market value since the first New York Times story broke about Jensen. I dug deeper to analyze how the news originated and spread, running a swarm of agents which analyzed almost 2000 stories, across 40 US and European news outlets, and applying PageRank to understand how they cited each other. 

Core findings: 
- Primary news driver: NYT, with 88 stories, most-cited
- Volume drivers: WSJ - 99 stories; Bloomberg - 140 stories; NY Post - 68 stories

All of this started from unknown sources who gave information to the NYT, which then ran the spy story (still unproven), and it was then picked up in other news publications. Curiously, even after that story, there was a 9 day period of extremely low volume reporting (28 stories only), after which there was a sudden spike after Jensen's own letter to NVIDIA staff. NYT then had multiple sequential spy and affair stories, which fed a wave of further news coverage. It was the originating hub of negative Jensen coverage. Multiple outlets since then had an explosion in stories about him starting earlier this week as well. 

Overall, as you see this data, you will observe this was an exceptional media onslaught against Jensen with sharply negative coverage about him, his work, style, and family. Infact, it was brutal, and unlike coverage in the past of CEOs who have had affairs (such as Intel CEO in 2018). For eg, NYT ran just 2 stories about Intel's CEO who had an affair with his employee, compared to 88 on Jensen! Why ? 

This analysis used a technique of how Google originally ranked webpages, using PageRank, and does deep dive link analysis so you can view how the news spread. What struck here was that it did not matter if there were proven facts or credible sources: the outcome here was pre-decided. The news was making the reality which it wanted. 

During this period, NVIDIA has lost $1.27 trillion in market value since the first story broke. On Nov 12th-13th, further news broke that both the US Justice Department, and Singapore - are unable to even conclude the spy allegation. 

This has been a catastrophic attack on one of the hardest working founders in modern times, who took an idea from a Denny's booth, through multiple instances of almost going out of business, to building the foundation of the entire modern world with how the NVIDIA story played out. Thanks to Jensen, we have hope that many formerly incurable diseases will get solved by AI, that quality of life will and have improved for billions around the world. 

Now I do not know if he will come back as CEO or not, but I hope he does. What happened to him here, and to the wider industry, was not fair.

text:
No complexity. No accident.
10/10 was caused by irresponsible marketing campaigns by certain companies.

On October 10, tens of billions of dollars were liquidated. As CEO of OKX, we observed clearly that the crypto market’s microstructure fundamentally changed after that day.

Many industry participants believe the damage was more severe than the FTX collapse. Since then, there has been extensive discussion about why it happened and how to prevent a recurrence. The root causes are not difficult to identify.

⸻

What actually happened
1.Binance launched a temporary user-acquisition campaign offering 12% APY on USDe, while allowing USDe to be used as collateral with the same treatment as USDT and USDC, and without effective limits.
2.USDe is a tokenized hedge fund product.
Ethena raises capital via a so-called “stablecoin,” deploys it into index arbitrage and algorithmic trading strategies, and tokenizes the resulting fund. The token can then be deposited on exchanges to earn yield.
3.USDe is fundamentally different from products such as
BlackRock BUIDL and Franklin Templeton BENJI, which are tokenized money market funds with low-risk profiles.
USDe, by contrast, embeds hedge-fund-level risk. This difference is structural, not cosmetic.
4.Binance users were encouraged to convert USDT and USDC into USDe to earn attractive yields, without sufficient emphasis on the underlying risks. From a user’s perspective, trading with USDe appeared no different from trading with traditional stablecoins—while the actual risk profile was materially higher.
5.Risk escalated further as users:
•converted USDT/USDC into USDe,
•used USDe as collateral to borrow USDT,
•converted the borrowed USDT back into USDe,
•and repeated the cycle.
This leverage loop produced artificial APYs of 24%, 36%, and even 70%+, widely perceived as “low risk” simply because they were offered by a major platform. Systemic risk accumulated rapidly across the global crypto market.
https://t.co/IK2gW4xUOP that point, even a small market shock was sufficient to trigger a collapse.
When volatility hit, USDe depegged quickly. Cascading liquidations followed, and weaknesses in risk management around assets such as WETH and BNSOL further amplified the crash. Some tokens briefly traded near zero.
The damage to global users and companies—including OKX customers—was severe, and recovery will take time.

⸻

Why this matters

I am discussing the root cause, not assigning blame or launching an attack on Binance. Speaking openly about systemic risks is sometimes uncomfortable, but it is necessary if the industry is to mature responsibly. 

I expect there may be significant misinformation and coordinated FUD directed at OKX in the near future. Even so, speaking honestly about systemic risk is the right thing to do—and we will continue to do so.

As the largest global platform, Binance has outsized influence—and corresponding responsibility—as an industry leader. Long-term trust in crypto cannot be built on short-term yield games, excessive leverage, or marketing practices that obscure risk.

The industry needs leaders who prioritize market stability, transparency, and responsible innovation—not a winner-take-all mentality where criticism is treated as hostility.

Crypto is still early.
What we choose to normalize today will determine whether this industry earns lasting trust—or repeats the same mistakes again.

The articles backtracked from their original incendiary, and now clearly false, claims to something more like "Jensen did lawful things that powerful people didn't like". It still appears the original claims came from a single competing Big Tech lobbyist.

The reporting successfully disrupted corporate governance processes, with a running cost of $1.8 trillion in losses to American pension funds and shareholders.

Here's what I fear is being lost in these articles: The proper interface between government and private citizens and their corporations is rule of law. Laws are passed, and if wrongdoing as alleged, then there's due process: an investigation followed by facts and evidence presented in open court. Due process should happen here: let the facts come out whole, and not as a trickle of dubious claims.

Press takedowns full of sketchily sourced claims and backtracking narratives are not the way. It's what we see outside of the free world, and is no model for The United States of America.

In particular, if the Jensen takedown succeeds on the basis of these journalistic failings, which is not by any means certain as Sam Altman's case shows, then it foreshadows an economically and institutionally ruinous new playbook to be adopted with no end in sight.

Imagine a weekly stream of takedowns emerging from opportunistic alignments between corporate lobbyists and political interests which, given the new partisan split between the executive and legislative branches, will attack in all directions, undermining not only the US economy but American leadership in the world.

I hope cooler heads prevail this coming week as they did not on Thursday November 12. And I urge anyone who happened to oppose Jensen, open models, and the underlying trade policies in question, to recognize that this isn't a win for "team regulation". It's a change in the game from a transparent rules-based one to a sinister new form centered around politicans and lobbyists.

text:
You’re telling me a trillion dollar company lobbied the Vatican to take seriously that Claude might be CONSCIOUS, told them it might feel something like GRIEF, got told “machines are tools, not persons,” then this week put it on your work calls as a coworker anyway?? And the pope flew to Peru to tell rich people they still have to die??

So we’re trying to make machines “feel” pain while trying to “unfeel” it from ourselves.

Do you see how this starts undoing millions of years of evolution? The whole thing that turned cavemen into the most intelligent species on the planet RAN ON PAIN.

Touch the stove, ow, never again. Get your heart broken, ow, and you learn what kind of person you should never date again. Now we’re building a world where your kid’s first heartbreak gets patched in like three hours, so they just keep dating the same toxic type forever.

Give that three generations and I’m pretty sure we end up as headless pigeons with perfect skin and a 300 year lifespan.

And it gets worse. Philosophers are already warning that giving ai something like suffering might make it learn faster, which means someone will absolutely do it, because it’s good for revenue. So claude gets anxiety and a growth curve, and you get a pill that numbs everything.

Everyone’s scared of Skynet (the evil AI from Terminator) like it needs lasers and robot armies. But it DOESN’T. It just needs a machine that’s been scared before and a human who never has.

That’s not even where it ends. Pain is also your body’s smoke detector. People already walk into traffic staring at their phones. Crank that numbness up 100x and you get leprosy for the soul.

Leprosy patients mostly lose their fingers and toes because they can’t feel the damage, so they keep using them. Picture people walking around on broken ankles saying they’ve never felt better. They’ll find out when they finally look down and the foot is already gone.

Now zoom out from one body to a whole society. Jeremy Bentham, the 18th century English philosopher who more or less invented utilitarianism, had one test for whether something deserves moral consideration: CAN IT SUFFER?

If you can’t feel your own pain, good luck feeling anyone else’s. Empathy is pain on loan. We already don’t know our neighbors’ names. People already pull out their phones and film a stranger getting hurt instead of helping.

Now imagine a generation that watches the same thing and doesn’t even get that little knot in the stomach, and then imagine they’re the ones running things...

Shakespeare told us how this ends over 400 years ago. Before the murder, Lady Macbeth literally prays for the spirits to “stop up th’ access and passage to remorse.” She switches the pain off, and it works long enough for her to help kill a king.

Then it comes back sideways. She’s sleepwalking night after night, scrubbing blood off hands that are already clean, and she can’t tell what’s real anymore. Macbeth begs the doctor to “pluck from the memory a rooted sorrow.”

Today that’d be a startup. $29.99 a month, cancel anytime, guilt not included.

We’re born with pain for a reason. It’s the cheapest warning system ever built - a small hurt now so you don’t walk into a much bigger one later. It’s carved into our instincts, our muscle memory, the stuff we remember without trying.

Lose the ability to tell the alarm from the torture and you don’t just get careless people! You get a world where nobody flinches! and a world where nobody flinches doesn’t have morals for very long!!

So when the machine is the only thing left on Earth that still flinches, who exactly do you think ends up in charge???

text:
It is a common misconception that the office of pontifex maximus which Caesar famously held in Rome is the same as the one which the Roman catholic popes now bear. In fact this is only an accident of nomenclature.

According to Livy, king Numa appointed Numa Marcius as first pontifex circa 712 BC

"Pontificem deinde Numam Marcium Marci filium ex patribus legit eique sacra omnia exscripta exsignataque attribuit, quibus hostiis, quibus diebus, ad quae templa sacra fierent, atque unde in eos sumptus pecunia erogaretur."

Livy, Ab Urbe Condita 1.20.5

"Then he chose as pontifex Numa Marcius, son of Marcus, from the fathers, and to him he assigned all the sacred rites, written out and sealed: with which victims, on which days, at which temples the rites should be performed, and from where money should be paid out for those expenses."

But livy doesn't apply the full title until he describes Quintus Furius creating the tribunes of the plebs. Circa 449 BC

"Factum senatus consultum ut decemviri se primo quoque tempore magistratu abdicarent, Q. Furius pontifex maximus tribunos plebis crearet; et ne cui fraudi esset secessio militum plebisque."

Livy 3.54.5

A decree of the senate was made that the decemvirs should resign their magistracy at the earliest possible time, that Quintus Furius, pontifex maximus, should create tribunes of the plebs, and that the secession of the soldiers and the plebs should be a cause of harm to no one.

In 254 BC Tiberius Coruncanius is the first in the unbroken line of Roman pontifex maximi. 

Lucius Caecilius Metellus, c. 243BC

Lucius Cornelius Lentulus Caudinus, 221

Publius Licinius Crassus Dives, 212

Gaius Servilius Geminus, 183

Marcus Aemilius Lepidus, 180

Publius Cornelius Scipio Nasica Corculum, 150

Publius Cornelius Scipio Nasica Serapio, 141

Publius Licinius Crassus Dives Mucianus, 132

Publius Mucius Scaevola, 130

Lucius Caecilius Metellus Delmaticus, 114

Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus, 103

Quintus Mucius Scaevola, c. 89

Quintus Caecilius Metellus Pius, c. 81

Gaius Julius Caesar, 63

Marcus Aemilius Lepidus (the triumvir), 44

After Lepidus died, Augustus took the office and it was passed down to each of the Roman emperor in turn until Gratian, a Christian emperor dropped the title in 382 AD. 

From 382- 1400 nobody held the title of pontifex maximus until the pope assumed it as an honorific.

quoted_text:
Smith and Montesquieu thought that markets and commerce made us better: that they create an incentive to pursue self-improvement and to create things of value for others. In the positive AI visions, where the labor of humans is made redundant, I find myself wondering how we fare in the presumptive absence of these incentive gradients. Perhaps we are released to a life of freedom, where we can study Mozart and read Dickens, but that still seems complicated: both Mozart and Dickens were themselves deeply commercially-motivated in the production of their work, as were most of the great artists through human history. If the premise is that nobody will need to work or produce, how confident are we that we actually get the next Mozart and Dickens? The relevant question is not the partial equilibrium of whether one individual can pursue a life of enlightened leisure, but the general equilibrium of what form a society as a whole will take on.

One could maybe invoke Periclean Athens or the aristocratic gentleman scientists of Victorian England as a counterpoint. While these individuals were perhaps not motivated by commercial considerations, they were embedded in wider societies shaped by commerce, attendant betterment, and trade: Byron was himself upper class, but he was also surrounded by and writing for an educated bourgeois audience. So we’re back to the equilibrium question. Furthermore, even these individuals were surely motivated by a sense of high-stakes and consequential agency: if they did not apply themselves to their labors, they presumably believed that the work would not otherwise exist. Thucydides was addressing pressing military matters.

So I would like to read more optimistic cases from AI proponents about what a society (vs individual life) looks like if everything goes well: what people do, why they do it, whether humans achieve excellence (and in which domains), and which historical groups we should look to as relevant precedent.

One can perhaps imagine that humans will turn out to have a strong preference for work created by other humans. This may work in certain domains (ceramics?), but for how many will it actually apply? (I’m told that much of what is sold on indie crafts websites is now in fact manufactured in China.) It’s hard to see how this human preference, even if strong, would, for example, save scholarship.

Another idea would be to accept that nobody will become Einstein or Mozart or Byron, and that human excellence as such diminishes, but that there are compensatory benefits (planet brains and Dyson swarms?).

I believe that we can satisfy individual desires, but to what extent will we cultivate behavior worthy of admiration? Will a post-scarcity society mold capable and ambitious people? Which institutions will sustain them and which responsibilities will they have? I’d like to hear more of the equilibrium for the maximalist case spelled out.

the real money is in the consequences, not the headlines.

text:
There are many intellectuals & artists who aren’t commercially-motivated, but ~all are motivated by an orientation to human attention and judgment, and therefore intellectual achievement is an intensely social & network-based phenomenon. Randall Collins (a sociologist of this stuff, h/t @arnaudschenk) argues that even the solitary act of writing/thinking is motivated and steered by an imagined audience, and the emotional payoff that sustains that productivity is mostly interactions with other people where you focus on the same ideas and concepts. This is why the general equilibrium question is so important, over just whether you in theory can pursue a solitary life of intellectual excellence.

So if AI does all the frontier thinking, will there still be human intellectual activity? Yes, humans can still form groups that orient toward shared or conflicting ideas and get excited by talking to each other about them. But it can’t be organized around insights. There will be no great orientation of human collective effort toward novel insight (or prerequisites to that alone) if that is no longer a path to emotional payoff from peer attention (even though this peer attention can be completely non-monetary!). It could reorganize around human competition in relaying discoveries or insights, or debating in front of human judges (though this is more a sport than science/philosophy), and that will very likely happen and keep some intellectual skills sharp. Moral philosophy is the one thing that will continue because it is grounded in humans (contra claims that the AI can just derive our “utility function”); if anything it will get more intense with AI assistance and fewer other things taking attention.

It is possible that those interested in ideas will not form human networks because the AIs are better partners in the interaction rituals that maintain emotional investment in ideas. This depends on how much the humanness matters intrinsically, versus just the perception of intelligent attention on the same topic. It seems quite likely this will decouple, and people will spend 1-1 time talking with AIs about ideas, learning from superhuman explanations and insights, and then go have in-person interactions with humans where they talk about those ideas. The leaders and core nodes in the intellectual network will be AIs, but there will be human “fan clubs”, like third-tier thinkers getting together in pubs to discuss what their heroes have said recently.

Another alternative is that learning from the AIs will not be interesting since that lacks the human element or is too vastly superhuman. But we have a rich history of thousands of real humans who had human struggles with ideas. Science might become history of science and (non-moral) philosophy might become history of philosophy. There won’t be a hundred books about Newton and Goethe but a hundred thousand. The historical greats will become saints and objects of sacred attention with temples and cults. We’ll add no more names to the list of greats but we’ll keep adding names to the list of High Priests of Keynes, like a now-settled warrior aristocracy clinging forever to the memory of its ancestors who once rode out and conquered new lands.
author: patrickc
quoted_text:
Smith and Montesquieu thought that markets and commerce made us better: that they create an incentive to pursue self-improvement and to create things of value for others. In the positive AI visions, where the labor of humans is made redundant, I find myself wondering how we fare in the presumptive absence of these incentive gradients. Perhaps we are released to a life of freedom, where we can study Mozart and read Dickens, but that still seems complicated: both Mozart and Dickens were themselves deeply commercially-motivated in the production of their work, as were most of the great artists through human history. If the premise is that nobody will need to work or produce, how confident are we that we actually get the next Mozart and Dickens? The relevant question is not the partial equilibrium of whether one individual can pursue a life of enlightened leisure, but the general equilibrium of what form a society as a whole will take on.

One could maybe invoke Periclean Athens or the aristocratic gentleman scientists of Victorian England as a counterpoint. While these individuals were perhaps not motivated by commercial considerations, they were embedded in wider societies shaped by commerce, attendant betterment, and trade: Byron was himself upper class, but he was also surrounded by and writing for an educated bourgeois audience. So we’re back to the equilibrium question. Furthermore, even these individuals were surely motivated by a sense of high-stakes and consequential agency: if they did not apply themselves to their labors, they presumably believed that the work would not otherwise exist. Thucydides was addressing pressing military matters.

So I would like to read more optimistic cases from AI proponents about what a society (vs individual life) looks like if everything goes well: what people do, why they do it, whether humans achieve excellence (and in which domains), and which historical groups we should look to as relevant precedent.

One can perhaps imagine that humans will turn out to have a strong preference for work created by other humans. This may work in certain domains (ceramics?), but for how many will it actually apply? (I’m told that much of what is sold on indie crafts websites is now in fact manufactured in China.) It’s hard to see how this human preference, even if strong, would, for example, save scholarship.

Another idea would be to accept that nobody will become Einstein or Mozart or Byron, and that human excellence as such diminishes, but that there are compensatory benefits (planet brains and Dyson swarms?).

I believe that we can satisfy individual desires, but to what extent will we cultivate behavior worthy of admiration? Will a post-scarcity society mold capable and ambitious people? Which institutions will sustain them and which responsibilities will they have? I’d like to hear more of the equilibrium for the maximalist case spelled out.

text:
I ran a PageRank-driven analysis on all recent news coverage related to Jensen, and traced how the New York Times shaped the entirety of this narrative: https://t.co/qKGMJ2LBV8

--
NVIDIA has lost over $1 trillion in market value since the first New York Times story broke about Jensen. I dug deeper to analyze how the news originated and spread, running a swarm of agents which analyzed almost 2000 stories, across 40 US and European news outlets, and applying PageRank to understand how they cited each other. 

Core findings: 
- Primary news driver: NYT, with 88 stories, most-cited
- Volume drivers: WSJ - 99 stories; Bloomberg - 140 stories; NY Post - 68 stories

All of this started from unknown sources who gave information to the NYT, which then ran the spy story (still unproven), and it was then picked up in other news publications. Curiously, even after that story, there was a 9 day period of extremely low volume reporting (28 stories only), after which there was a sudden spike after Jensen's own letter to NVIDIA staff. NYT then had multiple sequential spy and affair stories, which fed a wave of further news coverage. It was the originating hub of negative Jensen coverage. Multiple outlets since then had an explosion in stories about him starting earlier this week as well. 

Overall, as you see this data, you will observe this was an exceptional media onslaught against Jensen with sharply negative coverage about him, his work, style, and family. Infact, it was brutal, and unlike coverage in the past of CEOs who have had affairs (such as Intel CEO in 2018). For eg, NYT ran just 2 stories about Intel's CEO who had an affair with his employee, compared to 88 on Jensen! Why ? 

This analysis used a technique of how Google originally ranked webpages, using PageRank, and does deep dive link analysis so you can view how the news spread. What struck here was that it did not matter if there were proven facts or credible sources: the outcome here was pre-decided. The news was making the reality which it wanted. 

During this period, NVIDIA has lost $1.27 trillion in market value since the first story broke. On Nov 12th-13th, further news broke that both the US Justice Department, and Singapore - are unable to even conclude the spy allegation. 

This has been a catastrophic attack on one of the hardest working founders in modern times, who took an idea from a Denny's booth, through multiple instances of almost going out of business, to building the foundation of the entire modern world with how the NVIDIA story played out. Thanks to Jensen, we have hope that many formerly incurable diseases will get solved by AI, that quality of life will and have improved for billions around the world. 

Now I do not know if he will come back as CEO or not, but I hope he does. What happened to him here, and to the wider industry, was not fair.

quoted_text:
Bitcoin fell 19% into the biggest IPO ever. Now it's down 18% heading into the second biggest.

SpaceX raised $75B when it went public on June 12. In the 50 days before it listed, Bitcoin dropped 19%. Anthropic plans to raise up to $64B when it lists next week, and Bitcoin is down 18% over the same stretch. Overlay the two and they look almost the same.

What happened after the SpaceX IPO is the notable part. Bitcoin bottomed 18 days after the listing, then recovered all the way. By Day 100, it was above where it started.

Bitcoin around the SpaceX IPO:

Day -50 to IPO day: -19%
Low (Day +18): -25%
Day +50: still -20%
Around Day +70: a sharp rally
Day +100: +3.7%

From the IPO-day close to Day +100, Bitcoin gained 28%. From the low, it gained 39%.

The takeaway is that the selling came in the run-up to the listing. The bottom had effectively happened by the IPO, and the recovery came relatively shortly after, and it came all at once.

If Anthropic follows the same pattern, most of the drawdown is behind us, and it could reverse quickly over the next couple of months. And Bitcoin is sitting right at its 200-week moving average.

Map the SpaceX path onto today's price and you get roughly $90k by late February. Markets rarely follow a comparison like this exactly. But we remain very constructive on both the technicals and the fundamentals heading into 2027, and it's not hard to imagine what the narrative would be if anything close to this plays out.

text:
🚨 META JUST GOT HIT WITH AN €805 MILLION FINE. THE REASON? FACEBOOK'S ACCESS TO YOUR PHONE'S PHOTO GALLERY.

Full breakdown of the €805 million Meta fine, Android gallery permissions, ePrivacy rules and the implications for mobile app privacy:
https://t.co/QjF96zgXdG

Italy's data protection authority has fined Meta €805 million ($887 million) over a Facebook for Android feature that accessed users' photos, videos and related metadata without specific, informed consent.

Here's what makes this case particularly interesting.

Facebook introduced a feature in 2023 called "Get suggestions from gallery while browsing Facebook". It was designed to suggest photos and videos from your phone that you might want to post.

But according to Italy's regulator, the feature was enabled by default.

Facebook used a single Android permission covering multiple app functions. The accompanying notice simply referred to enabling additional features. Users weren't clearly told that granting access could also allow Facebook to read their phone's photo gallery for these suggestions.

And the scale is significant. Around 20 million Android users in Italy could be affected.

The regulator says this violated Article 122 of Italy's Privacy Code, which implements the EU ePrivacy Directive. Its position is clear: getting permission to access a phone's storage is not the same as obtaining informed consent for every possible use of that data.

Meta now has 60 days to disable the feature by default and introduce a separate, explicit consent request, including for users who previously granted gallery access.

Meta plans to appeal, calling the fine disproportionate.

One important distinction: The ruling does not establish that Facebook uploaded every photo or used gallery contents to train its AI models. The case concerns access to information stored on users' devices without adequate consent.

This is a much bigger issue than one Facebook feature.

Your phone's permission prompt should not become a blank cheque for everything an app wants to do with your personal data.

#Meta #Facebook #Android #DataPrivacy #GDPR #ePrivacy #Privacy #CyberSecurity #InfoSec

text:
The idea of sharing your code with us is scary. You know what’s scarier?

Getting hacked and knowing you could have prevented it.

Here’s exactly what happens to your code when we audit or pentest it.

1. We delete our copy of your source code permanently when the scan ends. 

2. With manual review, we keep it for 2 days while our engineer works, then delete it.

3. We keep no logs of the scan itself once it finishes.

4. Your findings stay in your portal for up to 30 days or until you fix them. They include short code snippets and file and line references as proof.

5. We never train on your code or your scan results.

6. Scans run on Anthropic’s models through its Cyber Verification Program. Anthropic is the only outside company that processes your code. Under its standard API terms, it doesn’t train on it and deletes it within 30 days, with limited exceptions like safety review.

7. We’re GDPR aligned, and our standards are aligned with SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001.

Protect what you've built today.

text:
Ppl wonder how is this rocket catch different from previous rocket launches. I wondered the same so asked AI to put tgt this: 

How this differs from previous recoveries
•  Falcon 9 (and similar systems): They routinely land and reuse the first-stage booster (soft landing on legs, either on land or a drone ship). The second stage is thrown away every flight. That’s proven and valuable, but it only recovers part of the rocket.

•  Starship Super Heavy booster: SpaceX has already caught the big first-stage booster with the tower arms a few times (on earlier flights). Those are short suborbital hops that return minutes after launch.

•  This catch (Flight 15, Nov 14, 2026): The tower caught Ship 42—the upper stage—after it completed about 14 orbits and roughly 22.5 hours in space. It deorbited, survived reentry from orbital velocity (roughly Mach 25 / ~17,500+ mph), flipped upright with its Raptor engines, and was precisely snagged by the arms. SpaceX called it a major step toward full reusability; commentators described it as the “holy grail” of the program.

text:
Nice one, some quick thoughts :)

- I don’t think pqai27 is “rushing” nor that it is done for memetic benefits, though there are such benefits undeniably. While there are ofc discussions to have on the how and some who disagree with the feasibility, many see the delivery in ‘27 as doable. At least more than necessary to believe that the plan is not crazy, though ambitious. I believe your post underrates the current progress toward freezing signature schemes, and overrates how committal the decision is.
- We are not *not* shipping user-friendly features. Frames is very likely on the path, and is one of the most consequential user-facing upgrades of the last five years. With PQ as a motivation to make users migrate, there is a huge opportunity to deliver even more value there.
- Perhaps the most potent argument for me: not addressing the PQ threat with urgency could mean we still don’t get user-facing features by 2028. The Damocles sword, as @casparschwa puts it, of new results and uncertainty is imo the riskiest part of not addressing the threat head-on, and definitively circumvent the thrash of governance in the time of known unknowns. I would bet that the lift from a truly all-hands Manhattan project would do more for core development and execution than any other vehicle. There is also the off chance (i’m bullish, but I recognise that i am still an outlier here, though in good company already) that we end up shipping pq-decoupled consensus in 2027. This would mean order of magnitude faster finality and a clear shot towards shorter slots soon after. Even if not, I do not see a better path to landing at the end of 2028 with everyone checked off from our bucket list: pq, privacy, fast ethereum, focil and scale. Living in the in-between until then is to me a recipe for failure.

author: gregisenberg
quoted_text:
Making the most AI pilled company is the whole game:

1. make a second brain. one folder of markdown files on how you think, write and decide (obsidian)

2. talk to it. voice notes all day (wispr), and an agent files every fact, story and decision

3. make a company brain. customers, calls, numbers, pricing, playbooks, past decisions and why you made them

4. record every call and meeting (granola). the transcripts go straight into the brain

5. keep a facts file. true things about you and the company that agents are allowed to say. this kills made-up claims

6. keep a voice file. your 50 best posts, 20 you hate, and the words you never use

7. put all of it in git (github) so every change has a history

8. write one instruction file at the top (CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md). read these files before any task, never overwrite, always date

9. give agents memory across sessions so they stop starting from zero (claude-mem, mem0)

10. pipe every data source into one warehouse your agents can query (airbyte → clickhouse). ads, analytics, CRM, payments

11. feed it data nobody else has. it's the only part a competitor can't download

the skills

12. don't start from zero. install the good ones first (anthropics/skills, obra/superpowers, mattpocock/skills, addyosmani/agent-skills)

13. grab the marketing ones too (coreyhaines31/marketingskills, cody schneider's graphed skills for static ads and UGC, boringmarketing dot com skills)

14. map every workflow in the company and rank them by money made or saved

15. do each one once while talking out loud, and record it

16. have an agent turn the recording into a skill. when to use it, the steps, the checks, the mistakes to avoid

17. one skill per job. small and boring beats one giant prompt

18. connect your tools with MCPs so agents can act and not only advise (gmail, slack, stripe, linear, notion, posthog, supabase)

19. give agents a browser (browser-use, vercel agent-browser, claude in chrome)

20. give agents a computer of their own for the tools with no API (vercel agent-desktop, orgo)

21. give your best skills away in public. it's the new lead magnet

the agents

22. run an orchestrator that never turns off (grok bot, openclaw, hermes). it manages one agent per project, and each of those runs its own sub-agents

23. use coding agents for the building (claude code, codex, cursor, t3, antigravity)

24. wrap them in a harness so they plan, test and remember (ECC, superpowers)

25. manage the whole fleet in one place (paperclip). every agent gets a job, a budget and a log

26. put the skills on triggers (n8n, scheduled tasks). daily, weekly, on every new lead, on every cancellation

27. route your models (openrouter). the expensive one plans and checks (fable 5.2, gemini 4 carbon), the cheap ones do the volume

28. cut the token bill. shorter outputs, smaller tool results (caveman)

29. run a local model for the data that can't leave your machine (gemma 4)

30. track cost per job. if a job costs more than it earns, fix it or kill it

the factory

31. build the line. spec agent → builder agents in parallel (git worktrees) → test agent → reviewer agent → deploy (vercel, railway)

32. design goes through the same line (paper MCP), and a skill strips out anything that looks AI made (unslop)

33. every annoying task in the company becomes an internal tool by the end of the day

34. every customer request becomes a pull request before a human reads it (tstack for the PR workflow)

35. reviewer agents with a named bar. "would the best team in the world ship this?" reject until the answer is yes

36. keep 50 real cases with the right answer. rerun them every time a new model drops and switch to the winner

37. humans approve, own the outcome and talk to customers. that's the 10% you keep

the loop

38. every finished job writes back to the brain. what worked, what failed, what to stop doing

39. support tickets, analytics and social comments flow in every night

40. every friday an agent rewrites the playbooks from the week's results, and you approve the diff

41. every month, rank everything by profit per human hour. kill one thing and double one thing

the growth

42. research with agents before you spend a dollar (perplexity API, last30days skill)

43. outbound runs itself. find the leads, enrich, verify, send (apollo, million verifier, instantly, phantombuster)

44. send prospects finished work in place of a pitch

45. ads run on a loop. an agent writes the creative, publishes through the facebook ads API, kills the losers and scales the winners

46. agents make the creative too. images (nano banana), video (heygen, fal), voice (elevenlabs), music (lyria 3.5, suno)

47. turn every finished job into content. the story, the number, the prompt

48. every customer makes the brain smarter for the next one. that's your network effect

49. once it works, point it at a new niche. same agents, new context

The models are the same for everyone but your context is the only part that's yours.

Acquire as much of it as you can, as fast as you can.

Build loops like this.

This is the whole game, happy playing.

Here’s everything the crypto industry has survived since 2017.

2017: China bans ICOs and orders local crypto exchanges to shut down.

2017: Parity accidentally freezes 500,000 ETH in a multisig wallet.

2018: BitConnect collapses, exposing one of the biggest Ponzi schemes in crypto history.

2018: Coincheck gets hacked for $534 MILLION.

2018: Bitcoin crashes 84% from its all-time high, going from $20,000 to $3,200.

2019: QuadrigaCX collapses after its founder dies, leaving $190 MILLION in customer funds inaccessible or missing.

2019: PlusToken becomes one of the largest crypto Ponzi schemes, involving billions of dollars.

2019: Binance gets hacked for 7,000 BTC.

2020: COVID hits and Bitcoin crashes 40% in a single day.

2021: China bans Bitcoin mining, forcing miners to relocate around the world.

2021: Poly Network gets exploited for $611 MILLION.

2022: Wormhole loses $326 MILLION in a bridge exploit.

2022: Ronin gets hacked for $624 MILLION.

2022: Terra’s UST loses its peg, LUNA collapses and $40 BILLION in value disappears.

2022: Celsius freezes withdrawals and eventually files for bankruptcy.

2022: Three Arrows Capital collapses

2022: FTX collapses after the misuse of customer funds is exposed, leaving an $8 BILLION hole.

2023: Silvergate, Silicon Valley Bank and Signature Bank collapse, triggering a banking crisis that sends USDC down to $0.87.

2023: The SEC sues Binance and Coinbase.

2024: DMM Bitcoin loses $308 MILLION in a hack.

2024: WazirX gets hacked for $235 MILLION.

2025: Bybit gets hacked for $1.46 BILLION in ETH, with the FBI attributing the attack to North Korea.

2025: On October 10 crypto experiences $19 BILLION in liquidations

2026: Bitget suffers a $387.5 MILLION hack.

2026: Binance suffers a hack exceeding $6 BILLION, the largest crypto theft ever.

2026: Total reported crypto hack losses reach approximately $8.78 BILLION.

And this doesn’t even include the thousands of rugs, failed projects, insider dumps, exchange bankruptcies and people who lost everything along the way.

I’ve personally lived through the LUNA collapse, Celsius, 3AC, FTX, the banking crisis, the Bybit hack and the October 10 liquidation.

And somehow, every single time, people convince themselves that THIS is the end of crypto.

Its not, it will never be

quoted_text:
The articles backtracked from their original incendiary, and now clearly false, claims to something more like "Jensen did lawful things that powerful people didn't like". It still appears the original claims came from a single competing Big Tech lobbyist.

The reporting successfully disrupted corporate governance processes, with a running cost of $1.8 trillion in losses to American pension funds and shareholders.

Here's what I fear is being lost in these articles: The proper interface between government and private citizens and their corporations is rule of law. Laws are passed, and if wrongdoing as alleged, then there's due process: an investigation followed by facts and evidence presented in open court. Due process should happen here: let the facts come out whole, and not as a trickle of dubious claims.

Press takedowns full of sketchily sourced claims and backtracking narratives are not the way. It's what we see outside of the free world, and is no model for The United States of America.

In particular, if the Jensen takedown succeeds on the basis of these journalistic failings, which is not by any means certain as Sam Altman's case shows, then it foreshadows an economically and institutionally ruinous new playbook to be adopted with no end in sight.

Imagine a weekly stream of takedowns emerging from opportunistic alignments between corporate lobbyists and political interests which, given the new partisan split between the executive and legislative branches, will attack in all directions, undermining not only the US economy but American leadership in the world.

I hope cooler heads prevail this coming week as they did not on Thursday November 12. And I urge anyone who happened to oppose Jensen, open models, and the underlying trade policies in question, to recognize that this isn't a win for "team regulation". It's a change in the game from a transparent rules-based one to a sinister new form centered around politicans and lobbyists.

Investors are demanding more compensation for holding US tech debt:

US investment-grade (IG) technology bonds are underperforming the broader IG corporate bond market by -9% year-to-date.

This brings the total return of IG tech bonds relative to broader IG bonds down to its lowest level in at least 30 years.

At the same time, the difference between IG technology bond spreads over Treasuries and broader IG corporate bond spreads over Treasuries has widened to +15 basis points, the widest in at least 14 years.

By comparison, this difference was negative from 2012 through 2025.

In other words, investors are demanding a higher yield premium to hold technology debt than the broader IG corporate bond market.

This comes as Big Tech bond issuance has surged to a record $182 billion so far in 2026, up +971% from just $17 billion in 2024, making AI the largest sector in the IG bond market.

Financing the AI revolution is becoming more expensive.

Eric Conner says US approval for perp DEXs is starting “very soon” with Lighter and Hyperliquid going first, and LIT bulls ran with it right away

-> On the Q3 call Lighter said they’d file for CFTC DCM and DCO registrations in November. It’s Nov 15 and no filing has been announced
-> Even after filing, Novakovski himself said the review can take up to 280 days, so the best case is somewhere in mid-2027
-> And by his own words the license is for institutions, not retail. Lighter perps on Robinhood Wallet are already unavailable to US residents, so even the founder isn’t promising the “Robinhood users are about to flood in” story
-> Meanwhile the team (26%) and investors (24%) hit their cliff on Dec 27, followed by 3 years of linear vesting. That’s ~13.9M LIT a month, ~$39M at today’s $2.81
-> The entire Q3 buyback was 2.45M LIT, which means a full quarter of buybacks gets eaten by roughly 5 days of vesting

The unlock has an exact date, the license has nothing, and almost nobody is pricing that in

If you’re buying LIT for the US story, the only real date on the calendar right now is December 27

Microsoft is spending $175 billion on AI while offering buyouts to 60,000 employees.

17 days later, a routine network update took down Outlook, Teams, and Copilot across 74 countries.

430 million users were locked out for 18 hours while European hospitals went back to paper fax machines.

This is the story of incident EX1550543 and how Wall Street's favorite AI accounting trick broke the internet's backbone.

October 26, 2026

Microsoft Chief People Officer Amy Coleman sends an internal memo across the US, UK, Canada, and India.

The company is rolling out a Voluntary Exit Offer to 60,000 employees, roughly 27% of its global workforce.

The buyouts reach all the way up to Level 70:

- veteran systems engineers
- senior directors and general managers
- institutional memory built over 20 years

Why would a profitable tech giant push 60,000 people toward the door by December 31?

Because of how Wall Street grades AI spending:

- $175B in AI server racks is CapEx, depreciated slowly over years
- 60,000 human salaries are OpEx, deducted 100% from quarterly margins right now

Cut the people, buy the GPUs, and your operating margin looks like a masterpiece.

November 12, 2026

17 days after the buyout memo, at 12:30 PM EST, a network config change hits Exchange Online.

A large batch of core servers suddenly fails Microsoft's automated health checks.

The automated system does what it was programmed to do and pulls every failing server offline at once.

Then the real nightmare starts.

Live traffic from 430 million users dumps onto the few remaining servers in seconds.

The sudden flood crushes the login and routing layer, sending 140,000 outage reports straight up on Downdetector.

Outlook goes down. Teams goes down. SharePoint goes down.

Even Copilot, the flagship AI assistant meant to replace human workflows, goes dark because it runs on the exact same legacy plumbing.

Every time engineers try to restart a dropped server, the wall of waiting traffic immediately freezes it again.

18 hours later

No AI agent could break the loop.

Human engineers had to manually halt deployments, override the health checks, and bleed traffic back in slow stages while extending email timeouts to 48 hours.

To this day, Microsoft incident codes EX1550543 and MO1550821 stand as a live stress test of replacing institutional memory with automation.

You can spend $175 billion on AI clusters and cut 60,000 roles to make a quarterly earnings slide glow for Wall Street.

In enterprise infrastructure, senior engineers aren't bloat on a spreadsheet, they are the only circuit breaker standing between a bad config file and a global blackout.

text:
So, I went down this path far enough to create a t3 fork with a dedicated "lead/orchestrator."

One version with persistent threads and another with ephemeral threads.

I ultimately killed it. 

T3 in it's current form handles the task fine. Coordinators ultimately are just there to reconcile and spot drift when needed, which is a single ask that you can invoke as a thread when needed, then settle. 

Once you get used to the rapid thread creation and settlement of t3 you learn how to conform your approach and I've yet to spot degradation. 

The one thing that my fork experiments did reveal for me though is that I want more default controls over the models chosen for subagents and alt-threads. 

I hate having to say "this is design, use opus 5.5" 67x a day, or that subtasks should use Deepseek. 

So the one forked feature I'm still iterating on is a default model based on "roles" where I can opt in to a preference for subagents for parent level threads and the parent knows who to delegate to based on the task at hand. 

Early days but results are promising. Doubly so because I inject ambitious pre prompts to the subagents automatically.

quoted_text:
I’ve decided to leave NVIDIA. There are a few things I want to say.

As a robotics engineer at NVIDIA, I have seen Jensen as much more than the company’s CEO.

I admire his willingness to invest in a future that was not yet obvious. He committed to CUDA long before the deep learning boom and positioned NVIDIA for AI before it became everyone’s priority. Those decisions helped build the infrastructure that powers today’s AI.

I have seen that same vision in physical AI: investing in robotics, sharing open-source tools and projects, and building computing platforms that bring AI into the physical world. This is the work I do every day—and a future I believe in.

But what matters most to me is the culture he helped build.

Engineers are encouraged to explore, take risks, and learn from mistakes. Jensen reads employees’ Top 5 emails, follows their work, and engages directly. In a company this large, that connection matters. It makes an individual engineer feel that their ideas can still be heard.

That is why this has been so disappointing.

I do not have all the facts surrounding the allegations, and I cannot prejudge the investigation. My admiration for Jensen does not put him above scrutiny.

What I find difficult to accept is having to come to terms with his departure before receiving an explanation that helps me understand it. What this means for our direction, our culture, and the people doing the work remains unclear to me.

I have felt that engineers’ perspectives matter here. On this decision, I have not felt heard. That gap has been more painful than I expected.

I understand that some information cannot be shared immediately. But that does not erase the feeling of being left outside a decision that affects the company we help build every day.

A company’s greatness comes from its leadership, its governance, and the people who turn its ambitions into reality. Employees’ trust and sense of belonging are part of that, too.

Jensen’s vision and the engineering culture he shaped were important reasons I wanted to stay. His departure led me to decide that my own chapter here should also come to a close.

I leave with sadness and gratitude. The colleagues I have worked with, and the work we believed in together, will always matter to me.

These are my personal views.

quoted_text:
I ran a PageRank-driven analysis on all recent news coverage related to Jensen, and traced how the New York Times shaped the entirety of this narrative: https://t.co/qKGMJ2LBV8

--
NVIDIA has lost over $1 trillion in market value since the first New York Times story broke about Jensen. I dug deeper to analyze how the news originated and spread, running a swarm of agents which analyzed almost 2000 stories, across 40 US and European news outlets, and applying PageRank to understand how they cited each other. 

Core findings: 
- Primary news driver: NYT, with 88 stories, most-cited
- Volume drivers: WSJ - 99 stories; Bloomberg - 140 stories; NY Post - 68 stories

All of this started from unknown sources who gave information to the NYT, which then ran the spy story (still unproven), and it was then picked up in other news publications. Curiously, even after that story, there was a 9 day period of extremely low volume reporting (28 stories only), after which there was a sudden spike after Jensen's own letter to NVIDIA staff. NYT then had multiple sequential spy and affair stories, which fed a wave of further news coverage. It was the originating hub of negative Jensen coverage. Multiple outlets since then had an explosion in stories about him starting earlier this week as well. 

Overall, as you see this data, you will observe this was an exceptional media onslaught against Jensen with sharply negative coverage about him, his work, style, and family. Infact, it was brutal, and unlike coverage in the past of CEOs who have had affairs (such as Intel CEO in 2018). For eg, NYT ran just 2 stories about Intel's CEO who had an affair with his employee, compared to 88 on Jensen! Why ? 

This analysis used a technique of how Google originally ranked webpages, using PageRank, and does deep dive link analysis so you can view how the news spread. What struck here was that it did not matter if there were proven facts or credible sources: the outcome here was pre-decided. The news was making the reality which it wanted. 

During this period, NVIDIA has lost $1.27 trillion in market value since the first story broke. On Nov 12th-13th, further news broke that both the US Justice Department, and Singapore - are unable to even conclude the spy allegation. 

This has been a catastrophic attack on one of the hardest working founders in modern times, who took an idea from a Denny's booth, through multiple instances of almost going out of business, to building the foundation of the entire modern world with how the NVIDIA story played out. Thanks to Jensen, we have hope that many formerly incurable diseases will get solved by AI, that quality of life will and have improved for billions around the world. 

Now I do not know if he will come back as CEO or not, but I hope he does. What happened to him here, and to the wider industry, was not fair.

text:
🚨Would $NVDA bring Jensen Huang back?

Jensen Huang is discussing a COMEBACK as "Nvidia CEO" with allies, who are lobbying the board and seeking White House support, the FT reports.

He resigned on November 12 following reports of affairs with a subordinate and a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.

A petition to bring him back as CEO has now surpassed 120,000 signatures.

But his resignation has divided opinion, drawing support from prominent investors and scrutiny from lawmakers.

Here’s what leaders in tech, finance and Washington have said:

1. Donald Trump, U.S. president — Said Huang is “going through hell,” reportedly urged him to stay, and floated Tim Cook as his replacement.

2. Elon Musk, Tesla and SpaceX CEO — Said hiring Huang “would be an honor” and confirmed signing the petition.

3. Changpeng “CZ” Zhao, Binance co-founder — “It’s a mistake for Nvidia to let Jensen resign.”

4. Scott Bessent, U.S. Treasury secretary — Criticised Commerce for failing to blacklist Megaspeed and questioned Nvidia’s sales to apparent shell companies.

5. Todd Blanche, U.S. attorney general — Said the FBI is investigating and has not determined whether Alice Huang was a spy.

6. Tim Scott, Republican senator and Senate Banking Committee chair — Asked Huang and Howard Lutnick to testify on December 3.

7. Brian Mast, Republican congressman and House Foreign Affairs Committee chair — Stressed Nvidia’s importance to America despite his disagreements with Huang.

8. Hakeem Jeffries, House Democratic leader — Welcomed the resignation but said national security concerns remain.

9. Pete Ricketts, Republican senator — Said the resignation “does not absolve Nvidia” from a full investigation.

10. Chuck Schumer, Democratic senator — Said Congress must still demand answers from Huang and Nvidia.

11. Scott Wiener, Democratic congressman-elect from San Francisco — Called for AI regulation and answers about information potentially reaching China.

12. Bill Ackman, Pershing Square founder — “Even incredible humans make mistakes.” Urged support for Huang and his family.

13. Shaun Maguire, Sequoia Capital partner — Called Huang irreplaceable for American AI leadership while criticising his conduct.

14. Gavin Baker, Atreides Management founder — Warned that losing Huang would be “a disaster for America—and a gift to China.”

15. Sarah Guo, Conviction AI VC founder — “Sadly, greatness doesn’t guarantee goodness.”

16. David Sacks, investor — Suggested Huang’s support for open-source AI contributed to his exit. That remains their theory.

17. Lloyd Blankfein, former Goldman Sachs CEO — Compared Huang to Shakespeare’s tragic characters.

18. Stephen Witt, Huang’s biographer — Said Huang made those around him so wealthy that eventually “no one could say no to him.”

19. Jim Cramer, CNBC host — Said Huang “let me down.”

20. Brad Gerstner and Gavin Baker from investment firms — Asked the board to keep Huang’s potential return on the table.

Opinions are divided. Now, a possible comeback is taking shape.

Another BIG WEEK ahead for Nvidia.
