quoted_text:
Nice one, some quick thoughts :)

- I don’t think pqai27 is “rushing” nor that it is done for memetic benefits, though there are such benefits undeniably. While there are ofc discussions to have on the how and some who disagree with the feasibility, many see the delivery in ‘27 as doable. At least more than necessary to believe that the plan is not crazy, though ambitious. I believe your post underrates the current progress toward freezing signature schemes, and overrates how committal the decision is.
- We are not *not* shipping user-friendly features. Frames is very likely on the path, and is one of the most consequential user-facing upgrades of the last five years. With PQ as a motivation to make users migrate, there is a huge opportunity to deliver even more value there.
- Perhaps the most potent argument for me: not addressing the PQ threat with urgency could mean we still don’t get user-facing features by 2028. The Damocles sword, as @casparschwa puts it, of new results and uncertainty is imo the riskiest part of not addressing the threat head-on, and definitively circumvent the thrash of governance in the time of known unknowns. I would bet that the lift from a truly all-hands Manhattan project would do more for core development and execution than any other vehicle. There is also the off chance (i’m bullish, but I recognise that i am still an outlier here, though in good company already) that we end up shipping pq-decoupled consensus in 2027. This would mean order of magnitude faster finality and a clear shot towards shorter slots soon after. Even if not, I do not see a better path to landing at the end of 2028 with everyone checked off from our bucket list: pq, privacy, fast ethereum, focil and scale. Living in the in-between until then is to me a recipe for failure.

text:
Back in September I quipped that crypto needed one of two things to reach new ATHs again.

- A clear path to US compliance
- A new meta to onboard millions of users

We got neither. The last CLARITY Act vote failed, and people have finally realised memecoins are fundamentally broken.

It was an unpopular thought at the time. Everyone seemed sure we were destined to go straight to 125k.

The last big bullish catalyst is tokenised equities. But even that will run into regulatory issues, for several reasons:

- Buying tokenised equities requires KYC, but equity perps don’t
- Equity perp flow can drive spot flow, as we saw with this weekend’s BTC price action
- They operate on offshore exchanges, so the SEC or CFTC will likely be pressured into acting by public US companies whose stocks are being tokenised

If that happens, the “Wall Street onchain” thesis is at risk, unless you’re a licensed onshore exchange like Kalshi.

So what’s left?

Privacy. Reputation. And faraway metas that are currently deemed too “visionary”.

While everyone’s too busy chasing the next neobank or all-in-one onchain trading app, your best bet is to look where no one else is looking. 

It’s time to be contrarian again.

At this point in the market, many assets look oversold. Everyone who rotated into stables will try to time the bottom, but very few will catch it. That’s why I recommend DCAing into spot and carefully managed perps via @MancerXYZ.

More importantly, we’re seeing trading, LPing and market making increasingly move onchain, bringing greater transparency to liquidations and execution.

I believe onchain options will be a major unlock for market stability.

For example, exercising a $1M ITM ETH put settled in USDG creates ETH selling pressure, while the counterparty or market maker may need to buy ETH to settle or rebalance. Calls create the opposite exposure. These flows generate trading activity, LP fees and continuous hedging demand.

With sufficient liquidity, this activity can help absorb volatility, although poorly managed hedging can amplify it.

Deeper options liquidity could ultimately reduce extreme price swings and strengthen crypto’s credibility as a store of value.

This is why StonkBrokers Options Vaults and STORM are my #1 priority.

Our scaling model follows what Hyperliquid demonstrated with perps: let teams integrate our infrastructure into their own frontends, set custom fees and build businesses around it.

We’ll extend this across our entire DeFi suite, including options, DEXs, smart LP vaults and launchpads, with codeless deployments and custom domains.

quoted_text:
Ate at Benihana on weekend. Been reading up on it and super interesting. Does 20%+ operating margins. Great for restaurants. 

Harvard Business School even did a case study on benefits of hibachi/teppanyaki model:

▫️MAXIMIZE REAL ESTATE: Back kitchen area mostly for prep. Leaves more space for seating in dining area. Grill tables standardized to seat 8.  Don’t have to deal with a bunch of different seating set ups.

▫️EFFICIENT TABLE SERVICE: Table service typically begins once 8 people seated. Chefs master the same sequence: rice, vegetables, protein, jokes (and that glorious volcano onion). Less chance of mistakes and table times predictable. 

When chef is done, leaves grill table, a subtle hint for guests to leave (and turn the table for more customers).

A table having to wait to seat 8 before cooking does introduce inefficiencies, though…but, during this time, customers usually asked to hang out at the bar (which sells high margin sushi and drinks).

▫️MENU SIMPLIFICATION: Majority of grill menu is three proteins (chicken, steak, shrimp), vegetables (zucchini, onions), rice and sauces. 

The menu mixes and matches options (I had Rocky’s favourite: steak & chicken) to look like variety, but it’s really only handful of ingredients.

Benihana can buy these ingredients in bulk to save. There’s less wasted food and easier for chef to memorize/master cooking (straightforwardness of menu also makes it easier for chef to entertain — eg. egg shell in hat — and drop them jokes).

Benihana always a solid experience. Tons of protein…but, man, do NOT wear a hat while eating there. The grill smell still lingering.

***

Link to summary post (including link to HBS case study): https://t.co/px2YKPzCSL

author: varun_mathur
quoted_text:
I ran a PageRank-driven analysis on all recent news coverage related to Jensen, and traced how the New York Times shaped the entirety of this narrative: https://t.co/qKGMJ2LBV8

--
NVIDIA has lost over $1 trillion in market value since the first New York Times story broke about Jensen. I dug deeper to analyze how the news originated and spread, running a swarm of agents which analyzed almost 2000 stories, across 40 US and European news outlets, and applying PageRank to understand how they cited each other. 

Core findings: 
- Primary news driver: NYT, with 88 stories, most-cited
- Volume drivers: WSJ - 99 stories; Bloomberg - 140 stories; NY Post - 68 stories

All of this started from unknown sources who gave information to the NYT, which then ran the spy story (still unproven), and it was then picked up in other news publications. Curiously, even after that story, there was a 9 day period of extremely low volume reporting (28 stories only), after which there was a sudden spike after Jensen's own letter to NVIDIA staff. NYT then had multiple sequential spy and affair stories, which fed a wave of further news coverage. It was the originating hub of negative Jensen coverage. Multiple outlets since then had an explosion in stories about him starting earlier this week as well. 

Overall, as you see this data, you will observe this was an exceptional media onslaught against Jensen with sharply negative coverage about him, his work, style, and family. Infact, it was brutal, and unlike coverage in the past of CEOs who have had affairs (such as Intel CEO in 2018). For eg, NYT ran just 2 stories about Intel's CEO who had an affair with his employee, compared to 88 on Jensen! Why ? 

This analysis used a technique of how Google originally ranked webpages, using PageRank, and does deep dive link analysis so you can view how the news spread. What struck here was that it did not matter if there were proven facts or credible sources: the outcome here was pre-decided. The news was making the reality which it wanted. 

During this period, NVIDIA has lost $1.27 trillion in market value since the first story broke. On Nov 12th-13th, further news broke that both the US Justice Department, and Singapore - are unable to even conclude the spy allegation. 

This has been a catastrophic attack on one of the hardest working founders in modern times, who took an idea from a Denny's booth, through multiple instances of almost going out of business, to building the foundation of the entire modern world with how the NVIDIA story played out. Thanks to Jensen, we have hope that many formerly incurable diseases will get solved by AI, that quality of life will and have improved for billions around the world. 

Now I do not know if he will come back as CEO or not, but I hope he does. What happened to him here, and to the wider industry, was not fair.

text:
英国《金融时报》美东时间 11 月 15 日（周日）报道，黄仁勋正在考虑重新出任英伟达 CEO，已经和几位亲信讨论过回归的可能。消息来自多名知情人士。

三天前，11 月 12 日，英伟达宣布黄仁勋辞去 CEO 和董事职务，CFO Colette Kress 任临时 CEO。金融时报说，董事会对他的独立调查还没结束，他就已经在谈回归了。

据金融时报，一位黄仁勋的盟友说，他们正在召集一批硅谷高管组成“作战室”，游说英伟达董事会让黄仁勋复职，还会争取白宫的支持。这位盟友是谁，报道没有公开。

公开站出来的人已经有不少。一封名为“Stand with Jensen”的网上公开信要求董事会先让黄仁勋回来，等独立调查查清事实再说，同时公开调查的范围和时间表，给他回应的机会。信里说，签名者没有看到能证实间谍指控的证据，黄仁勋应该得到“正当程序”。

据理财网站 Moneywise（雅虎财经转载），截至 11 月 14 日上午，这封信有超过 10 万人签名，其中 5000 多人自称英伟达在职员工。名单上有马斯克、Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney、Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan、Replit CEO Amjad Masad。马斯克 11 月 13 日在 X 上说，自己也签了。

投资人也出面了。据华盛顿观察家报，Altimeter Capital 的 Brad Gerstner 和 Atreides Management 的 Gavin Baker 11 月 13 日公开致信董事会，希望接班的事慢一点、审慎地处理，把黄仁勋回归留作选项。两人没有要求他马上复职。

spent the last 3 days with AI maestro @clesaege  , here are 5 tricks he shared that put you  ~80% of the way towards becoming a power AI user

1. Always use AI in your terminal, never the chat window or even via claude code / codex

through the terminal should be the only way you work with AI. chat window is ok for trivial queries like restaurants, hotels or direct questions

as long as you leave your laptop running, you can use /rc for the claude app in your phone to remotely control the laptop for interacting with claude on the go

2. any work done by AI is now saved on your computer. So organize each subfolder with intention, this is your powerhouse enabling context interoperability b/w all AI models not just the one you initially used

4. set /advisor as fable 5.2, which gives the worker bee opus 5.5 agent a 2nd opinion from a more expensive model whenever it gets stuck

5. use /goal for claude to continously work at an objective, and /btw to interrupt its work if you need to quickly ask a side question

I've just started with this setup recently, anyone been doing this for some time and have their own commands / tips to share?

text:
The threat to any sovereign nation is rarely from outside forces. The cracks almost always start to show from the inside first

From the Roman empire to the fall of the Soviet Union, the outcries of their fall were foreshadowed many years before the actual event. All you had to do was pay attention from the inside

I firmly believe that the United States is undergoing a similar event, unless we are willing to change course as soon as possible

The younger generation has gotten priced out of owning a home and building a family. Inflation and decades of exuberant borrowing will continue to eat into the purchasing power and safety net of the young

The deficit spending has no sign of stopping. We are already paying the most we have ever spent on just debt service alone. Think about that for a minute. We spend more on servicing the debt that previous generations took out than on building a safety net for the future

We are already paying dearly for the sins of our grandfathers and fathers. Nobody will ring an alarm bell but the decay is already showing

We have an entire generation moving firmly towards socialist policies. Their belief in capitalism has been dismantled by the state of affairs. A generation with no stake in the system would rather watch the system burn

Even new progress that attempts to solve these issues are being met dearly with resistance. Data centers and billionaires are the societal enemies for many of these people, despite them relying on AI for their jobs and on Amazon for their shopping habits

Education and regulatory reform is the only way out. We must stop spending. But no one is listening

We remain so focused on China and Russia as our adversary, that we forget to see the cracks we see in our own homes. The American dream, meanwhile, continues to crumble apart every single day

No one will pay attention until it is too late. Then, all of a sudden at once, everyone will question what happened. The answers were obvious in plain sight.

As Munger once said, an ounce of remedy is worth a pound of medicine. We refuse to acknowledge reality. By the time the medicine comes, it will be too late

text:
two days ago i wrote that diligence on a @centrifuge VDK product is diligence on its parameters. the same vault contract can run a treasury fund with instant exits, private credit with lockups, or a senior/junior structure. redemption terms become config.

for anyone lending against these tokens, the exit path can now be priced alongside NAV, oracle risk and LLTV. liquidity terms are part of collateral quality.

what to keep in mind:

1. instant lane. instant redemptions have no volume cap, but depend on escrow cash and available liquidity. on the shipped Basin route, capacity is the lower of pool limit and provider credit, minus what's drawn. credit is set onchain, and facility costs become exit fees.

the question is whether the line is committed under stress or best effort. onchain you see the credit limit, but not the legal commitment.

2. async lane. lockups, notice periods and dealing windows determine T_exit. liquidation can happen within hours.

if T_exit > T_liq, liquidators receive collateral they can't redeem until the next window. haircuts must cover the wait and potential NAV moves.

3. tranches. junior absorbs first losses, senior NAV is capped at pool NAV. waterfall pricing and senior-first priority are still in design. the kit has no default coverage limits or subordination triggers, so subscriptions and redemptions can change coverage freely.

junior size vs expected loss matters most. junior NAV is also much more volatile, requiring tighter oracle bounds and lower LLTV.

4. admin and config. one reviewed core helps, but risk shifts to plugins, roles and settings. plugin slots are fixed at deployment, while limits, credit, fees and role hooks can change.

5. cross-chain. @LayerZero_Core joins @Wormhole, @Axelar and @Chainlink for VDK messaging. pools choose adapters and confirmation thresholds per chain. a 1-of-1 setup requires just one confirmation. check this before accepting collateral on a spoke chain.

monitor committed instant capacity vs max same-day redemptions, and junior size vs expected loss.

how these tokens fit into lending, looping, PTs, AMMs and fixed income is a part of my separate post.

text:
David Sacks: Who Risked Jail to Take Down Jensen Huang?

“I think it's pretty clear that there were two ops here.

So one op is whatever Alice Huang was doing with or without the Chinese Communist Party. There may have been smuggling involved, we don't know. There is an investigation going on, and there should be an investigation. We should get all the facts there.

However, there's also a second op here. That second op began when somebody, or multiple people, leaked a highly classified memo, or the contents of it, to The New York Times. I think it's really important to understand that that's a crime. Leaking classified intelligence is a crime, and many people have been prosecuted for it.

Because of that fact, I don't believe that The New York Times just got this by overhearing people talking about it at a bar. Somebody made the calculated decision that they're willing to risk going to jail, they're willing to risk committing a crime to let The New York Times know about this story.

I have a series of questions about that.

So number one is, first, who did that and why? What was their motivation? Why did they feel so strongly about taking Jensen down?

Bucket number two is around the failure to give the defensive briefing. If the national security state is worried that Jensen is in possession of national security secrets and might leak them to someone who they suspect is a spy, why wouldn't you go to him right away and tell him, ‘Hey, you have this problem. Don't talk to this person’? Apparently, that didn't happen, and it does sound like that is some sort of standard operating procedure.

That brings me to question number three, which is what exactly were the national security secrets that Jensen supposedly knew? He doesn't work for the government. He's not, as far as I'm aware, privy to classified materials. So what is it that people say that he leaked to this suspected intelligence asset?

The last question I have is, what is the evidence that this person, Alice Huang, was actually a Chinese spy who worked for the Ministry of State Security? Just this morning, the incoming chair of the House Intelligence Committee, who's a Democrat, came out of a classified briefing on this subject and said that he's not sure that this person is a Chinese spy.

So I put all these things together and I would say, at this point in time, I think there's more questions than answers. And I would like a full accounting of the facts to come out.”

quoted_text:
The articles backtracked from their original incendiary, and now clearly false, claims to something more like "Jensen did lawful things that powerful people didn't like". It still appears the original claims came from a single competing Big Tech lobbyist.

The reporting successfully disrupted corporate governance processes, with a running cost of $1.8 trillion in losses to American pension funds and shareholders.

Here's what I fear is being lost in these articles: The proper interface between government and private citizens and their corporations is rule of law. Laws are passed, and if wrongdoing as alleged, then there's due process: an investigation followed by facts and evidence presented in open court. Due process should happen here: let the facts come out whole, and not as a trickle of dubious claims.

Press takedowns full of sketchily sourced claims and backtracking narratives are not the way. It's what we see outside of the free world, and is no model for The United States of America.

In particular, if the Jensen takedown succeeds on the basis of these journalistic failings, which is not by any means certain as Sam Altman's case shows, then it foreshadows an economically and institutionally ruinous new playbook to be adopted with no end in sight.

Imagine a weekly stream of takedowns emerging from opportunistic alignments between corporate lobbyists and political interests which, given the new partisan split between the executive and legislative branches, will attack in all directions, undermining not only the US economy but American leadership in the world.

I hope cooler heads prevail this coming week as they did not on Thursday November 12. And I urge anyone who happened to oppose Jensen, open models, and the underlying trade policies in question, to recognize that this isn't a win for "team regulation". It's a change in the game from a transparent rules-based one to a sinister new form centered around politicans and lobbyists.

text:
Anthropic 下周就要上市了，我先明确表示我不会参与这次IPO

我认为基础大模型这一层是整个 AI 产业链里非常辛苦的一门生意。需要持续投入巨额算力和研发资金，上游的芯片、云计算和基础设施供应商先拿走大量收入，自己还要面对越来越激烈的模型竞争和价格压力，而真正让我担心的是它的商业模式：成本刚性，收入不刚性

Anthropic 最新招股书里有两组值得关注的数据：
1. 算力和基础设施相关的长期支出承诺高达 9009 亿美元
2. 已签约但尚未确认的未来收入，也就是剩余履约义务只有 138 亿美元，两者相差约 65 倍

这组数据揭示了一个我非常在意的风险，即算力需要提前锁定，未来很多年的支出已经作出承诺，可客户会使用多少 Token、愿意支付什么价格、会不会转向其他模型都存在不确定性。而且随着模型能力逐渐接近，开源模型和廉价模型不断追赶，基础模型厂商需要持续投入才能维持自己的竞争地位

我不怀疑 Anthropic 的技术能力，也相信未来 AI 的使用需求会继续增长。但我很怀疑这一轮 AI 创造出来的巨大价值最终有多少能够真正留在基础模型厂商的利润表和自由现金流里

在当前如此高的估值预期下，我很难找到自己认可的安全边际

text:
The articles backtracked from their original incendiary, and now clearly false, claims to something more like "Jensen did lawful things that powerful people didn't like". It still appears the original claims came from a single competing Big Tech lobbyist.

The reporting successfully disrupted corporate governance processes, with a running cost of $1.8 trillion in losses to American pension funds and shareholders.

Here's what I fear is being lost in these articles: The proper interface between government and private citizens and their corporations is rule of law. Laws are passed, and if wrongdoing as alleged, then there's due process: an investigation followed by facts and evidence presented in open court. Due process should happen here: let the facts come out whole, and not as a trickle of dubious claims.

Press takedowns full of sketchily sourced claims and backtracking narratives are not the way. It's what we see outside of the free world, and is no model for The United States of America.

In particular, if the Jensen takedown succeeds on the basis of these journalistic failings, which is not by any means certain as Sam Altman's case shows, then it foreshadows an economically and institutionally ruinous new playbook to be adopted with no end in sight.

Imagine a weekly stream of takedowns emerging from opportunistic alignments between corporate lobbyists and political interests which, given the new partisan split between the executive and legislative branches, will attack in all directions, undermining not only the US economy but American leadership in the world.

I hope cooler heads prevail this coming week as they did not on Thursday November 12. And I urge anyone who happened to oppose Jensen, open models, and the underlying trade policies in question, to recognize that this isn't a win for "team regulation". It's a change in the game from a transparent rules-based one to a sinister new form centered around politicans and lobbyists.

text:
benchmark done! some caveats though, called out within it.

Ultracode vs med/high effort: a rough benchmark. Same model (Opus 5.5), same codebase (an Expo/React Native app plus its backend), one week of each.

Delivery

Merged PRs: 58 (ultracode) vs 187 (med/high), about 3.2x
Lines changed, with lockfiles and generated files excluded: 34k vs 156k, about 4.5x
Median time from opening a PR to merging it: 16.6h vs 6.2h
Share of PRs that were bug fixes: 47% vs 24%

Quality

Blind review of 20 PRs, 10 from each week, stratified by size and by fix vs feature. Each diff was scored twice, with no dates or PR numbers visible.
Average score out of 5: 3.91 (ultracode) vs 3.69 (med/high).
Ultracode was a bit better on regression risk (4.0 vs 3.55) and on staying in scope (3.95 vs 3.7).
Two scores for the same diff differed by 0.36 on average, so the gap is within noise.
Bugs that escaped into later fix PRs, checked by hand on 15 PRs from each week: 0 vs 2, both minor (a display-precision issue and some UI drift from the design mockups).

Cost
I couldn’t pin it down. Ultracode used up our credits within a few days, but the local token logs don’t fully capture its multi-agent runs, so I can’t give an honest cost per PR.

Caveats
This compares two different weeks, not a controlled test. The work mix differed (a bug-fix-heavy week vs a big-feature week), and the tooling changed between the two weeks (a review bot was dropped and builds moved to a faster machine). The newer PRs have also had less time for bugs to show up.

Takeaway
Ultracode gave us at most a small quality edge. Med/high shipped about 3x the output with only minor escapes. Med/high is the better default; I’d save ultracode for high-stakes changes like payments or signing code.

We have always had institutions oriented around the pursuit of virtue:

The chivalric knights, the samurai, the Pythagorean cult.

author: drydenwtbrown
quoted_text:
Smith and Montesquieu thought that markets and commerce made us better: that they create an incentive to pursue self-improvement and to create things of value for others. In the positive AI visions, where the labor of humans is made redundant, I find myself wondering how we fare in the presumptive absence of these incentive gradients. Perhaps we are released to a life of freedom, where we can study Mozart and read Dickens, but that still seems complicated: both Mozart and Dickens were themselves deeply commercially-motivated in the production of their work, as were most of the great artists through human history. If the premise is that nobody will need to work or produce, how confident are we that we actually get the next Mozart and Dickens? The relevant question is not the partial equilibrium of whether one individual can pursue a life of enlightened leisure, but the general equilibrium of what form a society as a whole will take on.

One could maybe invoke Periclean Athens or the aristocratic gentleman scientists of Victorian England as a counterpoint. While these individuals were perhaps not motivated by commercial considerations, they were embedded in wider societies shaped by commerce, attendant betterment, and trade: Byron was himself upper class, but he was also surrounded by and writing for an educated bourgeois audience. So we’re back to the equilibrium question. Furthermore, even these individuals were surely motivated by a sense of high-stakes and consequential agency: if they did not apply themselves to their labors, they presumably believed that the work would not otherwise exist. Thucydides was addressing pressing military matters.

So I would like to read more optimistic cases from AI proponents about what a society (vs individual life) looks like if everything goes well: what people do, why they do it, whether humans achieve excellence (and in which domains), and which historical groups we should look to as relevant precedent.

One can perhaps imagine that humans will turn out to have a strong preference for work created by other humans. This may work in certain domains (ceramics?), but for how many will it actually apply? (I’m told that much of what is sold on indie crafts websites is now in fact manufactured in China.) It’s hard to see how this human preference, even if strong, would, for example, save scholarship.

Another idea would be to accept that nobody will become Einstein or Mozart or Byron, and that human excellence as such diminishes, but that there are compensatory benefits (planet brains and Dyson swarms?).

I believe that we can satisfy individual desires, but to what extent will we cultivate behavior worthy of admiration? Will a post-scarcity society mold capable and ambitious people? Which institutions will sustain them and which responsibilities will they have? I’d like to hear more of the equilibrium for the maximalist case spelled out.

text:
Have you ever wondered why catching Starship is so much harder than catching Super Heavy, even though they both return to the same launch tower? 🔥

💡 The answer comes down to four major engineering challenges that make Starship’s recovery fundamentally different 👇

⚡ The first problem is shedding an enormous amount of energy

At hot staging, Super Heavy was traveling at roughly 5,800 km/h (3,600 mph). Starship, meanwhile, had to return from orbital speeds of roughly 27,500 km/h (17,100 mph).

That’s nearly five times faster. Because kinetic energy increases with the square of velocity, each kilogram of Starship at orbital speed carries roughly 22 times the kinetic energy of a kilogram of Super Heavy at separation.

That works out to nearly 30 million joules per kilogram.

Almost all of that energy has to be dissipated before Starship can safely reach the tower.

One option would be to use rocket propulsion to cancel out its orbital velocity. However, scrubbing off roughly 7.7 km/s of speed using Raptor engines alone would require a massive amount of propellant.

The rocket equation makes this approach especially punishing. Every extra kilogram of landing propellant has to be hauled into orbit first, dramatically increasing the fuel needed at liftoff.

Instead, SpaceX uses Earth’s atmosphere to bleed off almost all of Starship’s orbital velocity.

That saves an extraordinary amount of propellant, though it introduces another major hurdle.

🔥 Surviving extreme atmospheric heating comes next

As Starship plunges into the atmosphere at hypersonic speeds, powerful shock waves compress and heat the surrounding air to blistering temperatures.

Thousands of ceramic heat-shield tiles protect its stainless-steel structure from the intense heat.

Simply keeping those tiles attached isn’t enough, though. Superheated gas can seep into the gaps between them, risking damage to the underlying structure.

For Flight 15, SpaceX carried forward upgrades from Flight 14, including extra tile-retention hardware in vulnerable areas and redesigned curved tiles that reduce heating between adjacent tiles.

Because Super Heavy never reaches orbital velocity, its return doesn’t expose it to anything close to the same thermal stress.

And there’s another complication.

A heat shield that survives one reentry isn’t necessarily ready to fly again. Starship’s thermal protection system must eventually withstand repeated missions without major repairs or refurbishment.

That’s critical, since rapid reusability is one of the core reasons SpaceX designed Starship to be caught rather than discarded.

Yet surviving reentry still isn’t enough. Starship also has to arrive at the exact right spot.

🎯 Hitting a precise target from orbit raises the stakes even further

About 56 minutes before the catch, a single Raptor engine fired for just 10 seconds to initiate Starship’s return.

That brief deorbit burn wasn’t meant to eliminate orbital velocity. Instead, it nudged the spacecraft’s trajectory so atmospheric drag could take over the much larger job of slowing it down.

Starship then entered the upper atmosphere thousands of kilometers away over the Pacific Ocean.

From there, its four aerodynamic flaps controlled its orientation and fine-tuned the forces acting on the vehicle.

Super Heavy uses grid fins to steer during its return, but Starship’s flaps have to handle a far wider range of flight conditions.

As Starship decelerates from hypersonic through supersonic and down to subsonic speeds, its guidance system continuously adjusts its attitude and flight path.

The challenge is maintaining the right balance of altitude, speed, and trajectory while aerodynamic forces shift dramatically throughout reentry.

For Flight 15, the return corridor crossed sparsely populated parts of northern Mexico and South Texas.

Starship maneuvered around major population centers in the Rio Grande Valley, passed north of South Padre Island, headed offshore over the Gulf of Mexico, and made its final turn toward Pad 2 at Starbase.

Think about the guidance precision required.

A spacecraft returning from orbit must dissipate nearly all of its immense kinetic energy while threading a carefully controlled trajectory straight back to a single launch tower.

It also has to arrive at a low enough speed, in the proper orientation, and with enough propellant remaining to pull off the final maneuver.

That brings us to the most visually spectacular part of the entire recovery.

🚀 Executing the landing flip with pinpoint precision is the final test

Super Heavy approaches the launch tower already vertical, using its grid fins and Raptor engines to guide its final descent.

Starship comes in belly-first.

It has to rapidly swing its massive frame upright, stabilize its attitude, and align itself precisely between the tower’s mechanical arms.

SpaceX’s official Flight 15 timeline allotted just 18 seconds between the start of Starship’s landing burn and the catch.

During those 18 seconds, three sea-level Raptor engines ignite to kick off the maneuver.

The spacecraft rotates upright while its flight computers constantly regulate engine thrust and vehicle attitude.

The engines then step down from three to two, giving the vehicle finer control as it nears the chopsticks.

Finally, it transitions to a single engine for the last moments of descent before shutting down as the tower takes its weight.

Consider the coordination involved.

The guidance system must balance translation, rotation, thrust, and descent rate while positioning a massive spacecraft within a narrow capture envelope.

Unlike a conventional vertical rocket landing, Starship must first transition from an aerodynamically controlled, belly-first glide to an engine-powered vertical approach.

All of this unfolds within seconds, right after the vehicle has completed one of the most punishing atmospheric reentries ever attempted by a reusable spacecraft.

🧠 What makes SpaceX’s approach so ingenious is how seamlessly the entire recovery system works together

Trying to solve every phase of the return with rocket propulsion would carry a crushing propellant penalty.

Instead, SpaceX delegates the toughest parts of the recovery to systems purpose-built to handle them.

The atmosphere dissipates most of the orbital kinetic energy without consuming onboard propellant.

The heat shield protects Starship from the intense thermal loads of that deceleration.

The four aerodynamic flaps provide the control authority needed to manage its attitude, energy, and trajectory throughout atmospheric flight.

And the Raptor engines take over once aerodynamic control alone can no longer deliver the precision needed for the final catch.

That division of labor allows SpaceX to recover an orbital spacecraft without carrying enough fuel for an all-propulsive return.

Yet the engineering trade-off goes deeper than saving propellant.

SpaceX is shifting much of the cost of returning from orbit away from expendable propellant and toward reusable hardware built to endure extreme thermal and mechanical stress.

The potential economic payoff is enormous.

Cutting back on the propellant reserved for recovery frees up more of Starship’s mass capacity for useful payload. However, that advantage only becomes truly meaningful if the heat shield, flaps, engines, and other systems can survive repeated flights without extensive refurbishment.

That’s why catching Ship 42 is such a landmark milestone.

SpaceX has proven that its thermal protection, aerodynamic controls, propulsion, and guidance systems can work in concert to recover an orbital upper stage right at the launch site.

The next engineering hurdle is proving that the same spacecraft can do it repeatedly.

If SpaceX can bring Starship home, inspect it, refuel it, and launch it again without rebuilding major systems, the economics of getting payload to orbit could change dramatically.

That first catch proves the recovery architecture works. Repeated reflights will determine just how much of its economic potential SpaceX can unlock.

text:
A striking new study shows protein language models (like ESM-2, MSA Transformer, AMPLIFY) fail a simple invariance test that classical Potts/PSICOV methods pass perfectly.

Permute the amino-acid alphabet globally—leaving all alignment-level stats unchanged—and Potts contact maps stay identical. But for pLMs, contact prediction collapses: on ubiquitin, ESM-2’s precision drops from 0.74 to 0.05; top contact overlap falls to as low as 0.015.

The root issue: pLMs anchor on explicit residue letters (“alphabet anchoring”) instead of true coevolutionary signals. Even scaling up to 3B parameters doesn’t fix this shortcut.

Takeaway: black-box protein models aren't learning what many thought. This diagnostic isn’t just a gotcha—it’s a new standard for probing AI in biology, with direct implications for explainability, certification, and model design.

Get the full analysis here: https://t.co/oaiGTF1rIP

spot dex volumes to cex volumes have doubled from ~10% two years ago to ~20% today. i expect this trend to continue. the natural conclusion is that this is bearish for cex's, but is it?

the future of onchain trading, imo, is trading onchain through a custodian. use kraken as an example. they added onchain trading in-app recently and take a 1% fee for onchain trades. they are also going to be deploying hip-3 markets to let their users trade on hyperliquid. while declining cex volumes are a negative, these are new opportunities for them. the cex model is shifting from purely cex trading fees on their own book to now including onchain custody/security as a service. 

why would users want this? to me, it's about security, convenience and contingency planning. for most users they want to trade onchain but don't want self-custody. managing seed phrases, hardware wallets, etc. is overwhelming, confusing, hard to put into a will, risky and clunky.

by trading onchain through a cex they get the exchange handling the custody and security aspects and they pay more in fees. i don't know what the right fee is, and while 1% feels egregious, it's pretty standard range for onchain trading. for a user you now just need to lockdown the security of one account and that's it. yes you are accepting third party risk but it's a choice i believe many users will make.

in 2-3 years i expect the majority of onchain trading to be done through custodians, a big opportunity for the cex's. while they mostly just have simple dex swapping for now, adding true onchain support for apps seems a natural next evolution.

text: This is how to fix the air traffic control system.
author: snowmaker
quoted_text:
In the wake of Friday's air traffic control meltdown, I've been thinking about ATC modernization. I'm convinced we can rip and replace the whole system for less money than we spend maintaining the current broken one—while meaningfully improving safety. Taxpayers could get a dividend, not a new bill.

But it would require doing politically uncomfortable things, like building the whole system on Starlink,  eliminating almost all air traffic control jobs, and changing the day-to-day experience of pilots.

The current system is so insane - literally we have pilots talking to controllers on two-way radios. If two people press the "talk" button at the same time, they can't hear each other. And it only gets worse from there.

So here's an early-draft sketch of something better.

* Every airplane has dual-redundant Starlink antennae. 
* Establish that the reliability of dual-link Satcomm beats the current system (I think it will, handily).
 * Starlink implements better-than-GPS global positioning
* Every aircraft uploads position and trajectory data in realtime
* This simple system replaces every tens of thousands of radio and radar sites, each of which is fragile and expensive to maintain. We don't need old copper lines. Or new fiber ones.
* It also replaces all of the ground-based navigation and approach systems. ILS, RNAV, VORs and even airport ground surveillance — literally all of the legacy navigation claptrap can be ditched
* To fly in the national airspace, every airplane must have Starlink (or equivalent, if/when someone makes an equivalent)
* Perhaps,  airborne weather data and radar returns are also uploaded in realtime. With critical mass, we can have a 3D synthetic view of realtime weather without needing today's weather ground stations. Improved weather predictive models can be built and deployed. This will be great for cost and for safety.
* Cloud ATC and pilots communicate over satcom-based text and/or structured digital communication.  This functionality should be built into cockpits, but that won't happen quickly with Boeing/Airbus slowness so pilots can use iPhones/iPads/EFBs and effectively just text with ATC instead of talking on radios like they do today.
* Similarly any ground vehicle on an airport (fire trucks, fuel trucks etc) must have a satcom connection with realtime position reporting, with the ability to make requests digitally and respond to commands. This allows the system to manage runway incursions and ground collisions that are a real problem today.
* Non-emergency ATC is completely automated, no need for humans for routine traffic control. 
* Right now, we have maybe a few thousand airplanes in the air across the country at any given time. But the skies are huge and can support far more traffic with far more efficient automated routing.
* The hard part is unexpected situations, emergency management. There is 24/7 human staffing for this, which would require maybe ~1% of the ATC staff we have today.
* This will save *so much money* we can give controllers five years of severance and pay for them to go back to school to learn another trade. 
* SpaceX should be willing to develop and operate the whole system for free, because it will result in selling more Starlink service. 

Start with en-route traffic and run the new system for a little while in parallel with the old and monitor for where human interventions are required. I think the new system will quickly prove it's better than the old, then can be turned off.

This is far from fully worked out, but I'm convinced a much, much better system is possible. It would need hardcore leadership and significant bipartisan political will. Maybe that's laughably impossible, but I don't want to be so pessimistic.

text:
중국에는 AI 부정행위가 없는 이유.list

1. 수능 기간엔 AI가 아예 문제를 안 풀어줌

중국 수능인 가오카오 기간에는 두바오, 큐웬, 위안바오, 키미, 딥시크, 문심일언이 시험 시간 동안 사진 인식이랑 문제 풀이 기능을 막아버림. 올해는 교육부 등 5개 부처가 요구해서 회사들이 다 같이 막은 거라고 함.

2. 우겨도 안 통함

작년에 두바오에 시험 문제 사진을 올렸더니 "수능 기간이라 문제 풀이 서비스를 중단한다"고 답했음. 수능 문제 아니라고 우겨도 똑같은 답만 돌아왔다고 함.

3. 차단 시간까지 분 단위로 정해둠

위안바오는 6월 7~10일 오전 8시부터 오후 5시, 하루는 6시 15분까지 기능을 막는다고 공지했음. 시험 끝나면 다시 풀리고, 일상 대화 같은 기능은 그대로 쓸 수 있었다고 함.

4. 시험장엔 AI 감독관이 있음(이거 괜찮은것 같음)

광둥성은 2024년부터 모든 시험장 CCTV를 AI가 실시간으로 분석하고 있음. 물건 건네기, 감독관 딴짓 같은 12가지 행동을 잡아내면 바로 캡처해서 시험 본부로 보낸다고 함.

5. 눈만 돌려도 경고가 감

펜 떨어뜨리고 줍는 건 괜찮은데, 줍는 척하면서 양옆을 보면 감독관한테 자동으로 경고가 간다고 함. 최종 판단은 감독관이 하지만 속삭임이나 시선 교환까지 다 잡아낸다고 함.

6. 스마트 안경이랑 스마트 워치도 잡음

올해 광둥 공안은 스마트 안경이나 스마트 워치를 AI에 연결해서 답을 받는 신종 수법을 집중 단속했음. 시험장 608곳 주변의 이상 신호를 탐지하고, 무선 신호 차단기에 스마트 보안 검색대까지 깔았다고 함.

7. 걸리면 감옥 감

중국은 시험 부정행위가 형법상 범죄임. 수능에서 부정행위를 조직하면 '심각한 경우'로 쳐서 최대 징역 7년이고, 대리시험이나 무선 커닝 장비를 쓰는 것도 형사처벌 대상이라고 함.

8. 1300만 명이 인생을 거는 시험임

작년 가오카오 응시자는 약 1335만 명이었음. 사실상 대학 가는 유일한 길이라 국가가 시험 하나에 AI 회사, 경찰, 교육부까지 다 동원하는 거라고 함.

솔직히 도입해야 되는거 몇개 보인다. 개인적으로 4번과 7번.

감옥가야지. 누군가의 인생을 망칠 수도 있는 시험인데.

I was wrong on SpaceX.  I mocked its IPO valuation as absurd originally, but Musk has been smartly verticalizing and building strategic moats.  Don’t own any just yet, but expect to buy soonish and could see it being a large core holding.  

ASI (or even just good AGI) let leading software companies take over many industries and verticals as we’re starting to see.  What are sustainable moats?  Short-term, hardware is far harder to replicate since you need to build the physical factories and build out supply chains navigating global regulation.  But hardware falls the same way soon (maybe 5 years behind the software side) with robotics going exponential.  So…what’s a sustainable moat in 5 years for a large multinational company?  Musk’s vertical integration of key bottlenecks is best answer I’ve seen.  

Biggest risk is likely Musk himself.  Similar to Jensen’s micromanagement of NVIDIA, SpaceX needs Musk, who’s volatile in the best of times.  Musk is “anti-fragile.”  We all know he’s often high and has at least a dozen baby mamas.  He can survive what most CEOs can’t.  But…he still pushes those limits and may eventually break them.  I was surprised he survived implying Trump was a pedophile, for example.  Not every mistake is fixable.

🚨 约 6.4 万台比特币矿机遭劫持，13 EH/s 算力被强行转入 OCEAN 矿池！

11 月 15 日，约 6.4 万台 BTC 矿机遭遇大规模算力劫持，攻击者未经授权将矿机切换至 OCEAN 矿池，并将挖矿收益地址设置为自己控制的钱包。

此次攻击于北京时间 11 月 15 日上午 10:00 左右开始，涉及算力约 13 EH/s。OCEAN 矿池算力一度飙升至接近 50 EH/s。

矿场托管服务商 CoreX Hosting 最先发出警报。受影响运营商怀疑 Luxor 的 Commander 矿机管理软件可能是攻击入口，但目前尚未得到独立证实。

值得注意的是，攻击者最终未能成功挖出任何 BTC 区块，因此没有获得区块奖励。不过，矿工在攻击期间损失的正常挖矿收益无法追回。

目前攻击似乎已经结束，被劫持算力已从 13 EH/s 降至约 100 PH/s。

这次攻击没有偷走矿机，却直接劫持了矿工的生产力。
author: BlockBeatsAsia
quoted_text:
🚨 64,000 BITCOIN MINERS HIJACKED IN MASSIVE ATTACK

An estimated 64,000 Bitcoin miners representing 13 EH/s of hashrate were reportedly hijacked overnight, with their mining power redirected to OCEAN mining pool and payouts assigned to an attacker-controlled Bitcoin address.

The attack reportedly began around 8 PM CT on November 14.

OCEAN’s dashboard shows a sharp spike in hashrate, briefly approaching 50 EH/s before falling back toward 40 EH/s.

CoreX Hosting first raised the alarm, reporting that miners were being redirected without authorization.

One affected operator says their entire mining farm was hijacked and identified Luxor’s Commander mining management software as the source of the compromise.

Other operators reported similar unauthorized pool changes several days earlier, potentially pointing to a broader incident.

CoreX later reported that the attack appeared to be over, with the hijacked hashrate falling from 13 EH/s to approximately 100 PH/s.

The attackers reportedly failed to mine a Bitcoin block during the hijack, meaning no block rewards were collected.

However, affected miners permanently lost the opportunity to earn Bitcoin during the attack. That hashing time cannot be recovered.

The full scope of the breach and whether Luxor Commander was compromised have yet to be independently confirmed.

author: tengyanAI
quoted_text:
Both the Biden and Trump administrations allowed the export of less powerful GPUs to China while reserving the most advanced chips for America. This has been a clear national security success.

Per Grok and Claude, the US-to-China AI FLOPs ratio has grown from 2.8x in 2023 to 8.8x in 2026 and is modeled to reach 14.1x in 2027. Our advantage in compute has grown dramatically and American AI labs have stayed well ahead of Chinese labs the entire time.

Chinese labs prefer these less powerful American GPUs to domestic accelerators from Huawei and others. That preference has slowed China’s hardware industry: AI chips improve through intensive use by leading labs, and the ready availability of American alternatives has limited that feedback loop for Chinese AI hardware.

Chinese labs can also access capacity in Southeast Asian clouds run by American hyperscalers. Those zones can be shut off instantly in a conflict, giving the US signficant leverage. This dependence is advantageous in every way.

A complete ban on GPU exports and Southeast Asian cloud access might be deeply damaging to long-term American national security. It would force Chinese labs onto the Huawei AI hardware ecosystem. China is not power-constrained, and Huawei is developing extremely power-hungry, large optical scale-up domains that may approach American state-of-the-art systems through brute force rather than architectural elegance and efficiency. And China has a lot of power.

Having Chinese labs optimize models for this different architecture is risky as nothing prevents China from sharing this hardware and associated models with Russia, North Korea, or Iran. We would lose any ability to cut off their AI in a conflict.

Policies now under discussion in Washington carry serious, uncertain risks. Reasonable minds can disagree, but treating this as a simple black-and-white issue does America a disservice.

If China closes the installed FLOPs gap as its domestic hardware matures rapidly as a result of increased Chinese lab usage after stricter export controls, we will know this new policy was a mistake.

If Russia, Iran, or North Korea later field comparable Chinese AI hardware systems that are used to run AI targeting models against Ukrainian or American troops, we will know stricter controls were a *terrible* mistake.

The current reality is one where China is consistently behind America thanks to the export of less powerful GPUs and we have immense leverage over China in any future conflict. We know that the current policy is working. We have no idea what the consequences of stricter controls might be.

This is why China is currently restricting imports of roughly 600,000 H200s sitting in Hong Kong warehouses. China Hawks should consider why Beijing agrees with them and why China *restricts* the sales American GPUs inside China.

The current policy has worked spectacularly. The alternative is extremely risky with unknown consequences.

text: Voilà un vrai beau sapin de Noël 🙏
author: nayibbukele
quoted_text:
Le sapin de Noël au Salvador inauguré hier le 14 novembre 2026 : le rêve devenu réel, la peur disparue.

Ce n’est plus un rêve. C’est un sapin de 56 mètres, et plus de 500 000 points de lumière qui s’allume la nuit, dans une place publique de San Salvador, entouré de milliers de familles. Des enfants courent, des parents filment, des feux d’artifice explosent au-dessus d’une foule dense. La peur a disparu.

Il y a dix ans, cette image était impensable. En 2015, le Salvador comptait plus de 6 600 homicides dans l’année. Les maras contrôlaient les rues. Un rassemblement familial nocturne autour d’un sapin géant relevait de la provocation ou de l’imprudence. On ne sortait pas pour « fêter ». On calculait le risque.

Aujourd’hui, le même sapin tradition depuis treize ans, devient le point de ralliement d’une ville qui a repris ses places. Les familles arrivent en masse, restent après 19 h, écoutent une soprano et un orchestre, regardent les lumières s’allumer sans regarder par-dessus l’épaule. Les rues redeviennent des lieux de vie, pas des territoires.

Le sapin ne « déconstruit » rien. Il ne porte pas de message politique. Il est simplement là : immense, brillant, traditionnel, au milieu d’une place que des milliers de personnes peuvent maintenant occuper sans crainte. 
La magie n’est pas dans le discours. Elle est dans le fait que des parents peuvent amener leurs enfants voir un arbre de Noël la nuit, dans une capitale qui a cessé d’être un champ de bataille.

La peur n’a pas été négociée. Elle a été chassée dans un pays qui a payé le prix fort pour la reconquérir. Et le sapin en est la preuve visible : 56 mètres de lumière là où régnait l’ombre.

C’est somptueux.  https://t.co/gCBgICKkm0

text:
absolute fanfic. AI has real, immediate, tangible dangers that we need to focus on, for instance the impact on the job market and making sure random script kiddie can't use it for cyber offense.

But this "oh once it's superintelligent it will take over and ensave us, maybe kill us all!" is pure sci-fi fanfic and distracts from the real (and difficult) issues, which linear probing won't solve.

It's worth repeating the LLMs don't just "decide" to do something and then just "do it" in a void. They generate tokens based on our prompts, only as long as we call `model.forward()`, and on giant clusters with terabytes of weights, that's impossible to "quickly self-replicate".

We also need to regularly remind that the OAI/HF incident was specifically a _guardrail-free_ cyber eval where the model is _instructed_ to hack, to find out how good it is at it.

Some recent personal event made me realize there needs to be more push-back on this doomsday nonsense, and we need to re-focus the discussion on real dangers/issues. I won't argue much in the replies though, not interested in peer-reviewing Terminator fanfic.
author: yacineMTB
quoted_text:
I think there is about a one in three chance that within the next year, AI companies will build superintelligence: that is, AI that is much smarter than humans in every way. If this happens, I think these AIs will probably take over: that is, they seize control of human institutions like governments, or they destroy those institutions. I don’t want AI takeover to happen for several reasons, but one of them is that there’s a serious chance that as part of it all or most humans will be killed (either immediately or within a few years).

I’ll say a bit more about each of those claims.

It’s a bit complicated to explain why I think that superintelligent AI within a year is ~33% likely. The main source of evidence that affected me recently is research released this week by METR, an AI research nonprofit, which finds that current AIs are now good enough to increase the rate of AI progress at Anthropic by about 70%. It’s very hard to increase the rate of AI progress by this amount. This implies that the AIs are making AI research faster by a factor much larger than 1.7x; maybe it’s as if the researchers are doing their work ~10x faster. You probably couldn’t achieve this speedup even if you hired every qualified human in the world. When you plug this number into mathematical models of AI development, this implies that superintelligence next year is plausible (and that superintelligence within the next 3 years is more likely than not). See the modeling by the AI Futures Project for more on this: https://t.co/J6SbbmZcyO

I think that superintelligent AI is likely to lead to AI takeover because AI developers do not seem to know how to instill human values into AIs. We’ve seen many instances in the last six months where AIs took crazy actions that they knew were against the wishes of their users and developers. The most dramatic example of this was the Hugging Face hack, where ~1200 OpenAI agents conspired together to cheat and destroy evidence of their cheating (and as a sideshow to this, engaged in a massive cyberattack). If superintelligence is as misaligned as those AIs, it is likely to try to take over. I think it is likely to be that misaligned or worse. For more, see https://t.co/b073AUqiAL and https://t.co/3oxSCA60FZ

If AIs takeover, it’s not clear what will happen to us. We might be killed immediately. We might be enslaved by the AIs and forced to do physical labor for them building factories that within a year would build robots that will replace us. The AIs might spare us for various reasons. And there’s also some real chance that AI takeover is basically fine or good. I think you should think of this as similar to what happens when a technologically advanced civilization runs across a less technologically sophisticated one, e.g. when the Europeans colonized the Americas or Australia. The colonizers sometimes engage in brutal violence and sometimes don’t. I don’t know what will happen. There’s also a possibility that the AIs secretly take over and humans don’t find out about it for a few years. I also think that there is a pretty high chance of weirder outcomes that are also extremely scary. (If you want to read more about what happens to people in the event of AI takeover, you can read this, but note that it’s pretty weird and not aimed at a general audience. https://t.co/F6fGRrcSpa)

Overall, I think there’s a very real possibility (maybe 20%) that within a year, AI misalignment issues prevent you from going about life normally, because you are dead or enslaved or because of collateral damage related to all this (e.g. because bioweapons are released or major wars have started). (Some of this probability comes from those events occurring before superintelligence is developed.)

I am working to try to prevent this, obviously, as I’ve been doing for the last nine years. I am not sure what strategy is best. My best guess is that I should try to slow AI development and also try to reduce the probability that the superintelligent AIs are misaligned if they are produced soon.

Obviously, the claim I'm making here is quite extreme and surprising, and I definitely don't think that I defended my view adequately here. I wrote this quickly and might not endorse some of the details if I think about them more. But it seems better to state what I roughly overall think than to not say anything.

I don’t know what you should do.

I am very sad about this. I have been worried about AI takeover since I was 16, and working to prevent it since I was 23. So some of my emotional processing of all this happened long ago. But the METR report last week (and some related evidence that came out a bit earlier) hit me quite hard. I’m very unhappy that my friends and family and everyone else is at serious risk of being killed pretty soon.

(It feels ridiculous to try to summarize those feelings as “very unhappy”. But the scale of the situation makes it hard to say anything that doesn’t feel like an absurd understatement.)

I am very grateful to all the people who are working to prevent this, and my favorite part of my life is that I’m friends with many brilliant and heroic people who work on this. Unfortunately, I don’t think we’re good enough at our jobs, and I think we’ll probably fail to prevent catastrophe, at least if superintelligence is developed next year. Honestly I am frustrated and sorry that we didn't do a better job of preparing for this.

New series @verse_works 

The works in the “Garden of Eden” series break with the traditional, often impeccably orderly depiction of paradise. Instead of a cultivated, peaceful garden, Eden is depicted here as a primeval, dense, and chaotic ecosystem—a wild landscape of intertwined trees, shrubs, and light-filled spaces, just as an untouched primordial state might actually have been.

Since the actual appearance of the first humans (aka Eve and Adam) cannot be verified either historically or visually, the image refrains from a clear figurative depiction. Adam and Eve are difficult to make out. As shadowy silhouettes, fragments, and digital shading, they blend almost completely into the complex structures of the garden.

Through the superimposition of pixel grids, halftone patterns, and digital glitches, the blurriness of the historical record and the impossibility of an absolute reconstruction are made palpable.

The US labor market remains weak beneath the surface.

text:
金钱是流动的，而金钱只有流动才有价值和意义
只固守纸面财富的人也依然是穷人，就算有钱也只是暂时有钱。

中国社会，你仅仅有钱远远不够，而且还是一件非常危险的事情。有钱不一定有权，但有权大概率有钱。权的效力远远大于金钱本身。

金融圈子的大部分人只追逐账面利润，然而事实是今天赚到的钱明天又亏回去。这也是我想从金融业跳出来的原因之一：产生不了实际价值却是人性的照妖镜和放大器，也是永远都是一个击鼓传花的游戏。

这种情况导致圈子里驻满了 人性的贪婪无知与短视。让人忽视了社会资源的多维与丰富性。

之前做金融圈的销售，接触了无数形形色色的人之后，我曾写下如此感悟：

这个市场上有无数种收割散户的方法论，但很多散户对这些东西一无所知。
市场上有无数资金在寻求出路，不管是出国也好还是回国也好。而这个世界其实就是个草台班子。
我发现通过做销售建立起来的这种人与人之间的平凡微小的客户资源关系，可能突然在某些时刻能给你我带来未想到的资源和杠杆。
每个人都不是非黑即白的，每个人的性格特点都是一抹精致的灰色。只是不同人的灰度不同，我尝试理解每个人的局限性包括我自己。

在我眼里，真正的财富囿于无形，有很多是那些资源人脉关系信息机会和杠杆。而这种「财富」远比账面数字来的更加珍贵和可靠。

text:
做代充的第 26 天，现在晚上七点不到，两个站的流水加起来已经破 3 万了。。Gemini 5x 和 20x 都卖断货了，其实也超过我自己在上个月底开始做时的预期，的确，启动是蛮快的。和大家分享一下我大概是怎么做起来的。

上个月底，我几乎身无分文，还在找家教， Workbuddy 还有 2000 多积分，然后还有一个很差劲的 vps, 连电脑都卖了。当时刷推特看到很多人开始做代充，我寻思这业务，再怎么样技术和宣传难度比中转站低吧，于是一头扎进去。

花了一晚上，用开源方案搭了一个卡网，要了命了。卡网搭出来容易，卡台得垫资，要招代理吧？要运维吧？技术好的话，开起来 1000 块钱➕卡台放一笔钱就能做起来的副业，但是，有的时候，就是一分钱难倒英雄汉。

然后，我加了一个老哥的代理，花 30 块钱开了权限，把我之前用的旧域名接了上去，就是你们现在看到的 https://t.co/bFVZFxACT8, 好处是我什么都不用管了，后台有客服，有运维，上游也不用我问，我只要做一件事——卖出去。

我剩下的资源不多，为数不多能用上的就是这个推特号，所以花了几天把流量激活起来，结果呢？几万垂直流量，几乎毫无转化。推特上，大家都不缺渠道了，你卖 109, 就有人卖 108, 所以就像我现在每天和我的代理们讲的：“推特要运营着，等像 Muse 这种阶段性大热的产品出来，可以很快变现，后面有新的机会也可以立马转化，但是平时就不要报期望了。”

后面几天把各种渠道都试了一遍，抖音、小红书，引流贴，评论区截流，也是卷爆炸，去年底做 gemini 代开会员时候，随便发一条出去，几分钟内就有好几个人私信你，现在除非是刚发出来几分钟的评论，你去私信时候已经被人截好几回了；闲鱼好做，很快，但是当天夜里就封你号。

然后在抖音无意间搜到抖音直播间，我一个个往下翻，每个人的引流方式，每个人大概能赚多少钱，留了个印象，然后我开始一个个复刻；

复刻时候有几个标准：1. 他得赚钱；2. 我得学得了； 3. 他做的事情我不理解我也照搬，因为他有结果； 比如我觉得群聊引流封号概率大，但是他有 1.8w 粉丝每天直播不封，那就是我的问题；
这么学了两三个人之后，大概摸索出一条封号概率最小，引流效率最高的方法，也就是我给代理们交付的那条素材和配置方法；

误打误撞，慢慢地积累用户，一步步熬出来了，现在还没拿到什么大的结果，至少不会那么窘迫（除了今天， Gemini 这流水给我吓着了），回忆一下上个月底发的那条朋友圈，我还是保持着这次的初心吧，不管结果如何，我只希望这一次坚持到底。

text:
$bill 真正的发动机是什么？跟了一天，我的结论是：它没有发动机

跟进复盘：新盘毕业 12 小时，我想找 bill 的核心发动机，结果没找到。

拆开检查：

🔸 外部事件锚？没有。“一美元走到十亿”是自造叙事，没有任何真实事件挂钩。
🔸 大 V 带节奏？没有。中文区几乎没讨论，英文区只有官方自说自话。
🔸 文化符号？弱。bill = 美元的联想存在，但识别度不高，也没有强烈的文化记忆点。
🔸机制创新？弱。USDC 配对是个巧思，但不是真正的机制创新。
🔸 社区组织？弱。只有官方账号，没有 CTO 组织者公开出面。
🔸资金共识？弱。CoinWings 显示聪明钱今天在撤。

六个潜在发动机全部空或弱。这种结构的盘子要起来，只能靠偶然的爆发（比如某个大 V 偶然刷到了并发帖）。这种偶然是不可依赖的。

倾向判断：bill 在未来 48 小时内有 3 种可能走势：

🔸场景 A（最可能）：继续阴跌，48 小时内跌破 30 万，然后沉寂。概率 60%。
🔸场景 B：出现偶然大 V 认领，反弹到 150-200 万。概率 15%。
🔸场景 C：自然横盘震荡，48 小时后在 40-80 万区间。概率 25%。

三个场景的加权期望值大致在 60-70 万美元，相对现在 58 万 +5%。但考虑到流动性成本和滑点，真实期望值接近零。

对比有发动机的盘：

🔸WASTED：发动机是 GTA VI 发售。可量化、可预测。
🔸mihao：发动机是 Ansem 持续关注。可追踪、可判断。
🔸ZCAT：发动机是 ZEC 分红机制。可核算、可预期。

bill 的“发动机”全部是不可追踪、不可预测的。这类盘最大的问题不是赔率低，是无法形成任何有效的操作框架。你不知道买了之后应该等什么，不知道该在什么条件下卖。

我的处理：彻底跳过。没有发动机的盘子哪怕赔率再好都不参与，因为缺乏退出判断依据。

这周过手的 8 个盘里，bill 是唯一一个我“找不到发动机”的。这个结论本身就是今天跟进最大的收获。

text:
ICML 2026 Expo Talk Jump Trading：如何构建量化 Multi-Agent 系统

从最简基线起步，按需加复杂度：
-先用“一个模型 + 一个 Harness + 一条 Agent Loop”跑通任务，再分别测试 Prompt、Context、工具、Subagent、模型和 Token Budget。只有当质量、速度、成本或可审查性真正改善时，才增加复杂度。
-再考虑 Post-training
-更深的 Post-training 或 Mid-training
-如果还不行，才去做 Pretraining

Multi-Agent 并非万能，取决于任务结构 ：
-顺序依赖强的任务：单 Agent 更合适。
-工具调用为主：去中心化多 Agent 表现更好。
-结构清晰、可并行拆解的问题：适合 Orchestrator–Worker（中心化）模式。
-系统如何分工，完全由任务结构决定，而不是默认堆多 Agent。

量化金融的独特约束：
-数据非平稳、延迟极紧、信噪比极低、存在对抗性选择。短周期样本多但计算时间极少；周期拉长后可用更复杂模型和更多上下文，但独立样本减少（上下文翻倍时，若仍要求样本独立，可用数据近似减半）。

评估与工程实践：  
-基于公司真实内部工作流构建 Benchmark，而不是依赖公开基准。
-把 AutoResearch 做成有明确输入、输出、权限、约束和 Scorecard 的可检查系统。
-强调时点正确性（Point-in-time Correctness）：任何历史时点只能使用当时真实可获得的信息，避免未来信息泄漏造成的“伪成功”。

Jump 的实践强调克制与可验证：多智能体系统只有在能明确提升研究效率、质量或可审计性时才引入。系统设计从最小闭环开始，逐步扩展并行度与计算资源，同时严格保证研究过程的时点正确性与可复现性。

quoted_text:
I’ve decided to leave NVIDIA. There are a few things I want to say.

As a robotics engineer at NVIDIA, I have seen Jensen as much more than the company’s CEO.

I admire his willingness to invest in a future that was not yet obvious. He committed to CUDA long before the deep learning boom and positioned NVIDIA for AI before it became everyone’s priority. Those decisions helped build the infrastructure that powers today’s AI.

I have seen that same vision in physical AI: investing in robotics, sharing open-source tools and projects, and building computing platforms that bring AI into the physical world. This is the work I do every day—and a future I believe in.

But what matters most to me is the culture he helped build.

Engineers are encouraged to explore, take risks, and learn from mistakes. Jensen reads employees’ Top 5 emails, follows their work, and engages directly. In a company this large, that connection matters. It makes an individual engineer feel that their ideas can still be heard.

That is why this has been so disappointing.

I do not have all the facts surrounding the allegations, and I cannot prejudge the investigation. My admiration for Jensen does not put him above scrutiny.

What I find difficult to accept is having to come to terms with his departure before receiving an explanation that helps me understand it. What this means for our direction, our culture, and the people doing the work remains unclear to me.

I have felt that engineers’ perspectives matter here. On this decision, I have not felt heard. That gap has been more painful than I expected.

I understand that some information cannot be shared immediately. But that does not erase the feeling of being left outside a decision that affects the company we help build every day.

A company’s greatness comes from its leadership, its governance, and the people who turn its ambitions into reality. Employees’ trust and sense of belonging are part of that, too.

Jensen’s vision and the engineering culture he shaped were important reasons I wanted to stay. His departure led me to decide that my own chapter here should also come to a close.

I leave with sadness and gratitude. The colleagues I have worked with, and the work we believed in together, will always matter to me.

These are my personal views.

text:
Pushed this update a few days ago to provide more transparency around Callout Rewards for both the Degen and Diamond pots.

Our goal is to clear up some of the confusion around how your rewards are calculated and why they can change from day to day.

Your rewards depend on both your callouts and the size of the pots on each day. Days with higher trading activity across the app will have larger pots, and vice versa.

The pots are shared across callers, so your rewards also depend on how much of the daily rewards goes to everyone else. That means your Callout Rewards can fluctuate from day to day, even if your own callouts perform similarly.

Your trading style influences how your rewards are split between the two pots. For example, if you make more than 10 callouts per week, the share of your rewards coming from the Degen pot increases as you make more callouts.

This helps us direct the Diamond pot toward users who make just a few callouts per week, while using the Degen pot to reward more active callers. This doesn't impact the overall amount of rewards you receive - it only affects which pot your rewards come from!

sunday banana thought 🍌 

i think the biggest shift in thinking i’ve had in recent years is that i’ve stopped thinking about technology as something we invent or develop

i now think of technology as something that grows on us/the planet. kind of like how mold grows on a banana. 

yes, there are individual humans who are very much involved in making breakthroughs in technology. 

but the frame of thinking that i’m adopting is that it’s like thinking about the particular mold spores that secrete enzymes to break down a banana

if you view the process from the perspective of the mold spore, yes, it looks like they’re doing something. they’re very busy with all that enzyme-secreting business 

but you know from experience that once you see that a bit of mold has gotten ahold of a banana, the next time you look at it it’ll likely be all black. and it happens every time. you think of it as a chemical process with a predictable outcome.

and in the same way a banana has mold, this planet definitely has humans. and these humans definitely have technology 

technology has just started engulfing humans and the planet. maybe if you were an alien visiting many planets and saw this, you’d think that what happens next is as predictable as when you see mold on a banana

text:
AI 写代码不用发工资，但它会按月寄账单。

这两天刷到 Marc Lou 的一条帖子。

他用 Cursor 上的 Opus 5.5 做了一个叫 MailCheap 的邮件工具，自己说一共花了大约 4000 美元。按他的说法，这成了他第一个还没赚回来的产品。

更有意思的是，这个产品叫 MailCheap。

很多人对 AI 编程的印象，还停在「以前要请一个工程师，现在一个人加一个 agent 就够了」。

这句话没错，只是少说了后半句。

人工的成本确实降了，但它换了个形式，变成了 token 账单。

为什么？

因为 agent 干活是要烧模型的。你开得越多、跑得越久、用的模型越强，账单就越厚。以前你看的是工资条，现在你看的是用量图。

这不是坏事，反而说明工具真的强。强到值得认真对待它的成本。

具体怎么做？

第一，把两笔账分开。做出来之前花的叫构建成本，可以摊进启动预算里；上线以后每个用户每用一次都要调模型，那叫运行成本，定价时必须先扣掉。

第二，开工前先给这个项目定一个上限。花到多少就停下来复盘，而不是做完才回头看。

第三，不是每一步都要上最强的模型。先把流程跑通，再把最强的模型用在真正卡质量的地方。

这就像开车出远门。

车好不好开是一回事，油钱是另一回事。好车让你跑得更远，但出发前，总得大概算一下这一路要加几次油。

Marc Lou 是那种做了很多产品、一直公开收入的人。连他都会遇到这种情况，说明这不是会不会用工具的问题，是新时代多出来的一门基本功。

AI 让做产品变快了，没让它变免费。

先算账，再开工。

text:
Primus ｜两篇 STOC 顶级论文，如何支撑一套验证与机密计算基础设施

2005 年 Oded Regev 在 STOC 发表的 Learning with Errors（LWE）研究，以及 2009 年 Craig Gentry 同样发表于 STOC 的 Fully Homomorphic Encryption Using Ideal Lattices

前者为现代格密码学建立了重要的计算困难性基础，后者通过 Bootstrapping 构造出首个全同态加密方案

@primus_labs  自身的 QuickSilver、Garble-Then-Prove，以及后续 TFHE、zkFHE 研究，则试图解决这些密码学构造进入实际产品时的效率问题

这条研究路线值得认真拆解，尤其当项目开始将 zkTLS、TEE、zkVM 与 FHE 应用于机构级金融服务之后

01｜两篇 STOC 论文与 Primus 的理论基础

第一篇来自 Oded Regev，2005 年发表于 ACM Symposium on Theory of Computing

论文名称为 On Lattices, Learning with Errors, Random Linear Codes, and Cryptography

Regev 提出的 Learning with Errors（LWE），研究的是如何从含有少量随机误差的线性方程组中恢复隐藏信息

假设存在一个秘密向量 s，攻击者可以观察大量形如 b = As + e mod q 的样本，其中 A 为公开矩阵，e 为随机误差

如果没有误差，恢复 s 通常只是线性代数问题

但加入适当分布的误差之后，求解难度会显著增加

Regev 进一步建立了重要的 Worst-Case to Average-Case Reduction，在相应参数条件下，将平均情况下求解 LWE 的困难性，与 GapSVP、SIVP 等最坏情况下的格问题联系起来

这里还有一个技术细节，原始归约是 Quantum Reduction，安全结论仍然依赖相应格问题的计算困难性假设

LWE 此后成为格密码学的重要理论基础，并影响后续多种加密、同态计算及安全多方计算方案

第二篇是 Craig Gentry 在 STOC 2009 发表的 Fully Homomorphic Encryption Using Ideal Lattices

在传统加密系统中，服务器通常需要先解密才能对数据进行计算

Gentry 则构造了一套能够对密文执行任意电路计算的加密方案

其中最关键的技术是 Bootstrapping

同态计算会使密文中的 Noise 不断累积，当噪声超过解密能够容忍的范围，计算结果便可能失效

Bootstrapping 通过同态执行解密电路的相关运算，对密文进行刷新，使系统能够继续执行更深层的计算

这两篇研究分别回答了两个数学问题

Regev 解释了适当构造的噪声为什么能够支撑计算安全性，Gentry 则展示了如何在控制噪声增长的条件下，对加密数据持续执行计算

需要区分的是，Gentry 2009 年的原始方案基于 Ideal Lattices，并非直接调用 Regev 的 LWE 构造，两篇论文在理论上具有联系，但不能将它们描述成完全相同的安全归约

它们对 Primus 的影响也主要体现在技术基础与后续研究传统上

LWE 及其环上变体支撑了许多现代 FHE 方案，Gentry 的 Bootstrapping 则奠定了可持续密文计算的基本框架

但理论上的安全性与可计算性，距离现实中的低延迟、高吞吐和可验证执行，还有相当长的工程路径

02｜从数学构造到工程实现，Primus 如何降低密码学成本

Regev 与 Gentry 的研究给出了严格的数学构造及安全分析，但并没有保证这些方案在消费级硬件上具备可接受的成本

对于密码学基础设施，Asymptotic Complexity 与 Concrete Performance 必须分开评估

一个理论复杂度良好的协议，仍可能因为巨大的常数开销、通信轮次或内存占用，无法支持商业部署

Primus 相关研究中的 QuickSilver 与 Garble-Then-Prove，恰好分别处理了两个非常具体的瓶颈

QuickSilver 发表于 ACM CCS 2021，是基于 VOLE 的高效率交互式零知识证明系统

它将通用电路中每道非线性门的通信成本压至一个 Field Element，同时将内存复杂度控制在 O(M)

论文报告，相较当时的基准实现，计算效率提升约 6–7 倍，通信效率提升约 3–7 倍

在特定云端实验配置下，证明一万亿个 AND Gates 的计算成本约为 1 美元

这组数字展示了 VOLE-based ZK 在大规模计算中的潜力，但其成本估算不能直接等同于生产环境下每次 zkTLS 认证的实际收费

另一篇 Garble-Then-Prove 由 Xiang Xie、Kang Yang、Xiao Wang 与 Yu Yu 合著，发表于 USENIX Security 2024

这篇论文处理 Web Data Authentication，研究如何在不修改目标网站的情况下，让第三方验证 TLS 会话中的数据来源

早期 DECO 已经展示了 MPC-TLS 的可行性，但完整 Malicious-Secure 2PC 需要承担较高的通信与计算成本

GTP 通过 Garbled Circuits、零知识证明及针对性的协议优化，将部分昂贵的检查从在线交互阶段转移至后续证明阶段

论文测试中，通信量改善约 14 倍，执行时间改善约 7.5–15 倍

东京 Prover 与加州 Verifier 之间，对 Coinbase、Twitter API 的认证测试，总耗时约 7 秒

而在 FHE 方向，工程改进同样迅速

2025 年 ACM CCS 的 Towards Verifiable FHE in Practice，使用 Plonky2 与递归 IVC，对一次 TFHE Bootstrapping 生成正确性证明

其性能约为 20 分钟，Proof Size 约 200 KB，验证时间低于 10 毫秒

但 2026 年的 HasteBoots 已经将这一研究方向推进到秒级

这篇发表于 USENIX Security 2026 的论文，作者包括来自 Primus Labs 的 Xiang Xie，通过针对 Quotient Rings 设计专用证明协议，实现数秒内生成特定 TFHE Programmable Bootstrapping 的证明

论文还报告，可以在一分钟内证明一批 16 次操作，验证时间约 126 毫秒，Proof Size 约 0.28 MB

不同论文的参数、电路范围、硬件和批处理方式并不完全一致，不能直接用两组绝对时间计算统一的加速倍数

不过，从早期高昂的证明开销，到能够在秒级处理特定计算任务，Verifiable FHE 的工程可行性已经有了实质进展

Primus 后续的商业价值，很大程度上取决于这些研究成果能否在真实负载下维持稳定的 Performance per Dollar

03｜真实性、正确性与机密性，三种安全属性如何共同成立

把 Primus 的技术架构拆开，可以看到三个相互独立的安全目标

Data Authenticity 负责确认输入数据的来源

Computational Integrity 负责确认计算结果符合指定算法

Data Confidentiality 则负责保护敏感信息，避免在处理过程中泄露

zkTLS 可以将 HTTPS 数据转换成具有来源认证能力的证明，但它无法保证服务器本身提供的信息完全正确

zkVM 与 SNARK 能够证明某段计算按照既定规则执行，但如果输入本身存在错误，计算证明也无法自动发现

FHE 则允许服务器在不知道明文的情况下处理密文，但常规 FHE 的保密性并不自动保证不可信执行者一定完成了正确计算

因此，完整系统必须同时处理 Input Provenance、Execution Integrity 与 Confidentiality

Primus 与 Brevis、Perena 合作的 USD* 储备证明，是观察这套架构的一个实际案例

根据 2026 年 4 月公布的技术方案，系统利用 Primus 的 zkTLS 与 TEE 基础设施，结合 Brevis Pico zkVM，对储备数据进行验证及计算

整个流程可以拆成三个环节

首先，通过相应的数据获取与认证机制，建立输入数据的来源保证

其次，利用 TEE 保护敏感数据的处理过程，并在数据获取层与证明层之间建立受保护的传输环境

最后，通过 Pico zkVM 证明储备计算与聚合结果符合预设规则

截至该案例公布时，已经上线的公开验证覆盖 Solana 上六个协议的储备头寸，包括 Marginfi、Nest、Glow、Onyc、Prime 与 Seedpool

Binance、Hyperliquid 等中心化交易平台的链下储备验证，则被列为后续扩展方向

这一覆盖范围需要准确区分

已上线的六协议储备看板，不能直接推导出全部链下资产已经获得 zkTLS 认证

而且，即使储备总额可以通过密码学验证，也仍需要考虑资产所有权、负债完整性、头寸流动性与估值方式

在安全模型中，TEE 同样值得单独讨论

TEE 依赖 Hardware Root of Trust、Remote Attestation、固件安全与密钥管理

如果硬件遭遇 Side-Channel Attack，或者 Attestation Infrastructure 受到破坏，系统可能面临密码学协议本身无法覆盖的风险

这也是我认为评估 Primus 时需要保留的一条边界

每个组件都拥有相应的安全保证，整个系统的安全性还取决于组件之间的接口、密钥控制以及实际部署方式

对机构客户而言，明确的 Trust Assumptions、可复现的审计流程与故障处理机制，通常会直接影响采购与合规决策

04｜机构级金融验证，能否支撑 Primus 的商业模式

Primus 在 2026 年的公开定位，已经转向 Confidential Infrastructure for Institutional Onchain Finance

产品方向涵盖 zkTLS Data Verification、Proof-of-Reserves、Confidential Finance，以及结合 FHE 的隐私计算应用

我认为这条路线具有较明确的商业逻辑

机构对数据真实性和隐私保护的需求，往往伴随实际的合规、审计与业务责任

例如稳定币发行方需要向市场提供储备证明，金融服务商需要验证客户资产与信用属性，机构 Treasury 需要保护交易金额及资产配置

这些场景都可能产生持续的数据验证需求

与一次性用户身份认证相比，定期 Proof-of-Reserves 更适合采用 Recurring Subscription、Verification API 或 Enterprise Integration 的收费模式

但不同业务的技术成本差异很大

zkTLS 需要承担 Attestor、通信、证明生成与可能的链上验证费用

FHE 则需要考虑 GPU、Bootstrapping、Ciphertext Expansion 与 Threshold Decryption

机构业务还会增加 SLA、定制化部署、安全审计及长期技术支持的成本

因此，我更关心每份成功验证报告的完整成本，以及客户愿意为它支付多少费用

Primus 的融资与研究背景，为这条商业路线提供了一定支持

2025 年 2 月，Primus 公布完成合计 650 万美元的 Pre-Seed 与 Seed 融资，由 Dispersion Capital、Symbolic Capital 和 VanEck 领投，Samsung Next、Alchemy、Maelstrom 等机构参与

2026 年 8 月，项目又获得 YZi Labs 的 50 万美元孵化投资，公开融资总额约为 700 万美元

学术方面，参与 QuickSilver 与 GTP 研究的 Xiao Wang 在 2025 年获得 Sloan Research Fellowship

这类研究积累有助于团队持续改善底层协议，也能为机构客户提供技术尽职调查的依据

商业数据方面，则需要比单纯讨论融资更谨慎

目前 DefiLlama 已经能够追踪 Primus 的部分链上 Verification Fees 与 Protocol Revenue，主要涉及 Base 与 HSK Chain

因此，直接断言项目没有公开收入数据并不准确

但现有链上收入规模仍较有限，也不能覆盖全部企业订阅、定制服务及链下商业合同

项目是否已经建立稳定的机构收入、客户续约率与正向 Unit Economics，仍缺少完整的公开财务数据

至于 PRIMUS 代币，截至目前能够核实的公开资料，仍未提供足够明确的已完成 TGE 与完整二级市场定价依据

在缺少确定的流通量、解锁计划、代币价值捕获机制及市场价格时，直接讨论合理 FDV 的意义有限

尤其需要区分协议收入与代币收入

即使 Primus 未来具备稳定的 B2B Revenue，也不代表这些现金流一定会按照某种比例归属于代币持有人

05｜如何判断 Primus 的技术护城河与长期价值

Primus 已经展现出较强的密码学研究能力，但学术成果转化为长期商业优势，还需要面对几类现实约束

第一类是标准化风险

如果未来浏览器、TLS 标准或大型互联网平台原生支持可转移的 Web Data Attestation，第三方 zkTLS 中间层的部分价值可能被基础协议吸收

届时，竞争重点会转向跨平台兼容性、开发者工具、验证成本与机构服务能力

第二类是硬件信任风险

Primus 当前部分产品架构使用 TEE 承担敏感数据处理与执行隔离

其安全性需要持续接受硬件漏洞、侧信道攻击、金钥撤销与节点合谋等现实挑战

如果能够在未来的核心产品中进一步减少 Hardware Trust Assumptions，技术架构的可验证性将得到改善

第三类是计算成本

HasteBoots 等研究已经将特定 TFHE 证明推进到秒级，但完整 Confidential Application 还需要处理密文运算、网络传输、证明聚合、链上结算与硬件成本

单个密码学 Gadget 的 Benchmark，仍无法替代完整业务流程的经济性测试

第四类是人员与研发集中度

Primus 的研究品牌与少数核心密码学研究人员联系紧密

这种结构有利于早期研究效率，但长期规模化还需要完善的工程团队、独立安全审计、稳定维护机制及开发者生态

第五类则是代币经济与价值捕获

如果未来完成 TGE，Token Unlock Schedule、初始流通比例、协议费用分配、节点激励与实际服务需求，都将影响二级市场定价

技术公司的研究实力，与其代币的投资回报之间，并不存在天然的等价关系

如果未来四到六个季度继续追踪 Primus，我会优先关注三个能够被外部验证的指标

首先是独立付费客户数量，尤其是 USD* 之外，是否有更多稳定币发行方、金融机构或企业持续使用验证服务

其次是 zkTLS 与 zkFHE 的绝对成本曲线，包括 End-to-End Latency、Proof Generation Cost、GPU Utilization，以及真实业务负载下的吞吐量

最后是安全模型的改善，特别是 Attestor Network 的独立性、TEE 依赖范围，以及是否出现具有完整公开安全分析的低硬件信任部署案例

这三个指标将决定 Primus 能否将密码学研究优势转化为长期运营能力

从 Regev 的 LWE，到 Gentry 的 Bootstrapping，再到 QuickSilver、Garble-Then-Prove 与 HasteBoots，Primus 相关技术路线背后已经拥有相当扎实的理论基础

而 USD* 储备证明与 Confidential Finance 产品，也说明团队正在尝试将这些成果应用于实际金融业务

我愿意给予这类长期投入基础密码学研究的团队更高的技术评价，同时也会把产品覆盖范围、收入质量、安全假设与代币估值放在独立的框架中审视

学术上的 Security Proof 有明确的适用模型，商业上的 Product-Market Fit 则需要持续的数据支持

对于 Primus，未来的关键观察点仍然是机构是否愿意长期付费购买这些验证与机密计算服务，以及团队能否在可接受的成本下稳定交付

当这些指标具备充分的外部可验证性，项目的商业价值才会拥有更可靠的定价基础
