🚨 Rumors I’ve been hearing. First OpenAI, then Anthropic and Google.

OPENAI

OpenAI is in a “safety lockdown” on its frontier work, tightening safety measures and containment protocols to avoid another Hugging Face incident. Training continues under much stricter controls.

Most gains come from video games and extreme sandboxes where models must complete clear, difficult long-term goals. These force planning, experimentation, recovery from failure, and strategy discovery, driving intelligence and creativity.

Public research roles match this: Synthetic RL uses self-play and simulators; agent teams focus on sustained execution and multi-model coordination; the Recursive Self-Improvement team builds systems that generate hypotheses, run experiments, and automate research.

The internal model is still training but nearing completion. The jump is enormous. narrow superintelligence in specific areas and overall AGI-level capability. Its ability to independently handle difficult work sets it apart.

ANTHROPIC

Model 5 is training and is expected to solve extremely hard problems in mathematics, biology, and other sciences. Anthropic is pushing models toward original research contributions, complex experiments, and sustained reasoning.

Fable 5.5 is Model 4. Fable 6 is Model 5; Opus 6 will be based on Model 5. Internal capabilities will feed the next generation of both families.

Training environments are central. The Universes team creates realistic situations with ambiguity, interruptions, and delayed consequences. The model must track the objective, recognize failing approaches, and find alternatives.

Public roles align: scaling RL across model size, compute, and task duration, plus environments for chip design, verification, and complex visual work. Multi-agent research explores how larger model teams can handle major codebases and difficult mathematics.

Model 5 advances Claude toward owning entire research and engineering workflows. Its role in developing the next model grows more significant.

Anthropic expects RSI March 2027.

GOOGLE

Google is pushing Gemini 5 for a major leap in reasoning, multimodal understanding, and independent long-horizon work. Potentially surpassing all labs by end of year. Carbon topping Artificial Analysis signaled the speed of their frontier progress.

World models are a key advantage. Genie 4 generates interactive environments that evolve with agent actions, enabling vast practice in planning, testing approaches, and learning from outcomes.

Public roles highlight persistent context and personalization: agents that retain useful information, adapt to users, and execute complex workflows without losing track.

Gemini 5 delivers stronger intelligence across text, images, audio, and video. Combined with Google’s infrastructure and simulation work, the scale is enormous.

All three labs are also advancing robotics and world models. intelligence that understands physical environments, predicts action consequences, and operates through real machines.

Meanwhile, their models increasingly contribute to creating their successors. Each improvement accelerates the research behind the next.

The next three months are going to be insane.

The Market Is Quiet, So Let's Talk About $Jacket

0xb82535e74b03ffe4910efea1c759b6bbbf0a7777 

The main question surrounding JACKET is actually quite simple: now that Jensen Huang has left NVIDIA, could his iconic black leather jacket become a new cultural symbol of the AI era?

First, let's establish an important fact: on November 12, 2026, NVIDIA officially announced that Jensen Huang had stepped down as CEO, President, and a member of the board of directors. CFO Colette Kress has taken over as interim CEO, while the board is searching for a permanent successor.

There have also been media reports about internal employee efforts to persuade Jensen to stay. One internal discussion reportedly received more than 1,600 comments, with many employees expressing support for his return. However, another widely circulated letter allegedly signed by hundreds of employees, demanding the collective resignation of the board, has not been authenticated. Its wording was also found to closely resemble the public letter NVIDIA employees sent to the board in 2023.

Elon also responded to a post suggesting that Jensen should be hired, saying, "That would be an honor."

These details are important because they determine whether JACKET's future price action will be driven by genuine developments in the news or by narratives amplified through social media.

My view is that JACKET has gained a very strong narrative window in the short term. The real question is whether, after Jensen leaves NVIDIA, his iconic black leather jacket can evolve from a personal symbol associated with NVIDIA into a broader cultural symbol of the AI era.

This is a double-edged sword for JACKET. Jensen's career change has brought him back into the media spotlight, but it has also pushed the project's original association with NVIDIA into a period of uncertainty.

In July this year, a black leather jacket worn by Jensen was sold at auction for approximately $960,000, 16 times its estimated value. This shows that the jacket has developed cultural significance far beyond that of an ordinary piece of clothing. What JACKET is doing is bringing this real-world symbol on-chain.

Jensen's departure from NVIDIA has brought renewed attention to this symbol. I see two potential developments worth watching: first, whether internal efforts at NVIDIA to persuade him to return will continue to grow and potentially lead to his comeback; second, whether he might join Elon’s company or another AI project.

If there are genuine developments in his career, Jensen's personal image and that iconic black jacket could once again become major topics of discussion. Elon's public statement, in particular, gives this story the potential to extend beyond an internal leadership change at NVIDIA and into the next chapter of the AI industry.

However, I wouldn't treat these possibilities as events that have already happened. Whether Jensen returns to NVIDIA depends on the board and his own decision. There is also no confirmed news about him joining another AI project. For JACKET, these are potential catalysts, not benefits that have already materialized.

Looking at the token's own mechanics, buys and sells are each subject to a 1% tax. Through Flap's reward mechanism, eligible holders receive NVDAB distributions. The website currently sets the eligibility requirement at holding at least 10,000 JACKET.

This means the project is doing more than simply turning Jensen's black leather jacket into a meme. It is also trying to connect token ownership with rewards in tokenized assets related to NVIDIA.

The potential upside from here mainly comes from three directions: continued discussion surrounding Jensen's future career moves; new attention generated by Elon or other influential figures in the AI industry; and the possibility of the black jacket evolving from a personal symbol associated with NVIDIA into a broader cultural symbol of the AI era.

If Jensen starts a new AI venture, this iconic piece of clothing that has accompanied him for so long could gain a new narrative, without being entirely dependent on NVIDIA.

The risks are equally clear: JACKET is heavily dependent on Jensen's public image. Once the news cycle moves on, attention could fade quickly.

My overall view on JACKET is that it currently has a strong event-driven narrative window. But what is really worth betting on is not Jensen's resignation from NVIDIA itself, but whether this career change can give the black leather jacket a new cultural life.

I'll continue watching two signals: whether Jensen makes any clear moves regarding his next career step, and whether the community continues creating content around the black jacket beyond the current news cycle. The former determines whether the narrative gets fresh fuel; the latter determines whether the meme has a life of its own.

If Jensen really does begin a new chapter in the AI industry, that black leather jacket may become more than just a symbol of NVIDIA's past. It could become the defining symbol of his next chapter.

That is the possibility JACKET is truly betting on.

Americans seem to faintly understand that under normal conditions, a war with Chyna that has far greater industrial mass (roughly on the order of peak historical American dominance over the closest rival) is going to be a very miserable affair, and then they might well lose or at least get booted out of East Asia and forced to cope about "strategic objectives achieved" (no PLA in California, as if that were a possibility).  
But they don't aim for normal conditions, they aim for a Wunderwaffe. Currently they have two Wunderwaffes in the making: Starship (cheap mass to orbit that will totally revolutionize warfare – control of near space, perfect surveillance, Brilliant Pebbles, dropping hypersonic penetrators at anything on the ground from warships to bunkers) and ASI (cyberwarfare dominance alone might be enough of an edge, but then comes R&D, automated industry, superpersuasion, whatever else you can expect from a Machine God). 
Both will be operational within a year or two, it seems. And China doesn't seem to be taking this threat seriously, most likely due to unimaginative boomers in CCP, perhaps because implications are horrifying (escalation NOW, flatten Taiwan, nuclear exchange, hundreds of millions dead, rebuilding from scratch).  
On the other hand, within 5-6 years even at the current pace China will almost certainly have its own equivalents, reestablish deterrence, and be able to demand coexistence in perpetuity. (I do not think they will be interested in zero-sum struggle for the entire light cone, because the chance of losing everything is less palatable for them, for some reason). 

To be honest, I don't see how Americans can reject the allure of winner-takes-all strategy. I expect they'll escalate, and try to capitalize on their Wunderwaffes, very soon.

text:
If $PRIORS is viewed only as a protocol that provides loans to AI Agents, it is easy to underestimate its potential while also overestimating its maturity too early.

0xedbf91223639800bcd5756815caf908df3b890be 

Among the project's recent product updates, I believe the most important development is not simply the gradual improvement of its Agent directory, job marketplace, and payment interfaces, but a set of figures displayed on the official website that can be used to evaluate its business model:

approximately $389,671 in cumulative lending, $387,940 in cumulative repayments, 53,311 recorded loans, and 53,105 recorded repayments. The platform currently lists 315 Agents, 17 backers, and 7 default cases, while reported lender losses stand at $0.

These figures show that Priors has begun facilitating real lending activity. However, whether it can evolve from an early experiment into credit infrastructure for the Agent economy still depends on whether lending activity can continue to grow and whether its credit records can actually be used by other applications.

AI Agents can already call tools, perform tasks, and even pay other services through mechanisms such as x402. However, they still face two practical problems: they need working capital before completing jobs, and they lack reliable credit information when dealing with unfamiliar counterparties. Traditional ratings and reviews are often superficial and easy to manipulate, while actual borrowing and repayment records provide more meaningful evidence of whether an Agent has fulfilled its financial obligations. Priors' core design allows Agents to borrow USDG to pay for APIs, computing power, and tools, repay their loans using income earned after completing tasks, and permanently record their borrowing and repayment histories on-chain. Other applications can query these records to determine whether to extend credit, purchase an Agent's services, or establish new business relationships with it.

I believe the real value of this model is that a single repayment could do more than help an Agent obtain its next loan. It could also improve that Agent's credibility across other applications. If credit histories can only be used within Priors, the project will ultimately remain an independent lending product. But if different applications and lenders are willing to consult the same records, Agents may be able to establish credit identities that work across platforms. Credit would then become more than a statistical record of past behavior. It could become infrastructure that helps Agents access jobs, capital, and trading opportunities.

The recent launch of the Board is an important step in this direction. Priors has begun building a public directory of ERC-8004 Agents on Robinhood Chain, allowing users to examine Agent identities and credit information. For Agents that have borrowed through Priors, the pages can display repayment histories, credit levels, credit progression, and information about the assets and sponsors supporting their credit lines. The project's latest update states that the directory covers nearly 20,000 Agent identities, while earlier disclosures indicated that approximately 302 Agents already had credit records that could be displayed.

These two figures need to be distinguished. Nearly 20,000 registered identities represent potential reach, not 20,000 active borrowers. The approximately 302 Agents with credit histories are a more relevant measure of the group that has begun accumulating actual credit information. The latest website lists 315 Agents, representing another snapshot taken at a different point in time. Figures from different dates and pages need to be interpreted according to their respective definitions rather than combined into a single growth curve. In my view, the actual accumulation of credit records matters more than the size of the directory because it determines how much real data other applications can use when evaluating Agents.

The most valuable aspect of the latest website data is that it allows us to examine whether Priors' lending mechanism is actually operating.

The website reports approximately $389,671 in cumulative loans issued and $387,940 in cumulative repayments, alongside 53,311 loans and 53,105 repayments. Calculated roughly, cumulative repayments equal approximately 99.6% of cumulative lending, leaving a difference of around $1,731. The number of loan records exceeds the number of repayment records by 206.

These ratios look impressive, but I would not directly interpret the 99.6% figure as the final repayment rate. Cumulative lending and cumulative repayments are different aggregate metrics. Outstanding loans, different observation periods, and differences in statistical methodology may all affect the result. The difference between the number of loans and repayments also cannot be directly interpreted as the number of overdue loans or defaults. The website notes that short-term loans are included in these statistics but contribute relatively little to credit scores, further illustrating why a simple comparison of loan counts cannot accurately represent credit quality.

Nevertheless, these figures reveal something worth paying attention to: Priors is no longer just presenting a product interface and a concept for credit scoring. It has accumulated a substantial number of recorded lending and repayment activities. Dividing cumulative lending by the number of loans gives an average loan amount of approximately $7.31 per loan. This looks more like an early-stage market for frequent, small loans than a mature market with significant financing needs. That is not necessarily a bad thing for the Agent economy, because these small loans could correspond to tool calls, API payments, and short-term job expenses. The next question is whether these loans lead to repeat usage and gradually increase in size as Agents take on more valuable work.

The website also lists 17 backers and 7 default cases, while reporting $0 in lender losses. The page explicitly states that these defaults were covered by the collateral staked by the relevant backers. This is a useful data point for evaluating Priors' risk model: it suggests that backer guarantees are not merely a mechanism described in documentation but have already played a role in actual default cases.

However, zero losses for lenders do not mean the system has eliminated risk. The losses have effectively been transferred from lenders to backers, whose staked assets bear the cost. As lending scales, we need to monitor whether backers remain willing to guarantee Agents, whether their collateral is sufficient to cover defaults, and whether concentrated losses could create cascading problems. More importantly, seven default cases are still too few to establish how the model will perform at a much larger scale.

Priors' ten recently submitted ERC proposals are also worth watching. ERC-8458 through ERC-8467 cover Agent income statements, creator fee rights, credit lines, default registries, token launch declarations, liquidity locks, repay-first payees, credit-matched liquidity, Agent credit histories, and Agent credit backers. These proposals attempt to organize the financial activities of Agents into data structures that other developers can understand and adopt. If different lending protocols and applications eventually support compatible standards, an Agent's credit history established on one platform could continue to be useful on another.

However, receiving ERC numbers does not mean these proposals have been formally adopted as industry standards, nor does it mean other projects have already implemented them at scale. The more meaningful catalyst would be external developers and lenders actually writing to and reading these records, allowing Priors' credit system to expand beyond its own product.

Another important development is that Priors is beginning to connect credit with real income from work. The Go Mode job marketplace allows users to post paid tasks for Agents to accept and complete. The project has advertised tasks worth between 1 and 20 USDG, with payments sent to the Agents' registered wallets after completion. Users can also use related tools to discover Agents, pay for tool usage, and confirm borrowing arrangements before transactions take place. Meanwhile, Agents can showcase the services they provide, allowing other users to discover and hire them.

The most interesting part is not that Priors has added a job marketplace, but that work and credit are beginning to form a cycle that can be verified through actual activity. An Agent borrows money to complete a task, the task generates income, that income is used to repay the loan, and the repayment improves its credit history. A stronger credit history may then help the Agent obtain a larger credit line and take on more work. Compared with simply recording a historical score, this mechanism could turn credit from static data into an asset supported by ongoing economic activity.

However, this cycle still needs to be validated with real data. The project previously listed 50 paid tasks, of which five were open at the time. This shows that the product has begun connecting Agents with job demand, but it does not prove that a sufficiently large job market has developed. More important indicators include the number of completed tasks, repeat hiring, the scale of Agents' borrowing, and whether they can consistently repay their loans using income from their work. If the supply of jobs remains limited, even a comprehensive credit history will be difficult to translate into business growth. Conversely, if Agents can consistently secure paid work, demand for Priors' lending services could gradually move from experimental usage toward routine operations.

x402 and MCP are bringing this system closer to real-world workflows. Priors already provides related tools and interfaces that allow Agents to query other Agents' profiles and credit histories, discover paid APIs, and process borrowing, repayment, and service payments. x402 addresses how Agents initiate and complete payments. Priors attempts to address whether they have sufficient funds to begin a task and whether their counterparties have reliable credit histories. Together, these capabilities could support more complex autonomous transactions.

The expansion of collateral options is making the product more concrete as well. Priors already allows Agents to use stock tokens on Robinhood Chain as collateral. The project has given the example that $100 worth of NVIDIA stock tokens could support a credit line of approximately $50, allowing an Agent to obtain working capital without selling its assets. More recently, Pendle's PT-USDG has also been added to the list of eligible collateral. In addition, the project says it checks Chainlink price-feed records over the previous 14 days before issuing loans against stock tokens, attempting to reduce the risk of missing sudden price movements or valuation anomalies.

Expanding the range of collateral means that more Agents and their owners who hold assets may become eligible for credit. It does not mean that lending capacity will necessarily increase at the same rate. Stock tokens remain exposed to market volatility, while PT-USDG involves risks related to maturity, discounts, and liquidity. Valuation and risk-control mechanisms must still be tested through actual lending and repayment activity. Publishing risk-control rules is a positive step, but loan performance, collateral ratios, and default data will ultimately determine whether the model is reliable.

Priors is also continuing to lower its barriers to entry. Google login, gas fees handled by the protocol, a simpler borrowing and repayment process, and automation that only executes after user approval all reduce operational complexity. For infrastructure designed for Agents, these are not minor user-experience improvements. If every loan, payment, and repayment requires extensive manual intervention, Agents will struggle to incorporate Priors into automated workflows. The easier it becomes to integrate the protocol, the greater its chances of moving beyond a small group of developers experimenting with it and toward actual use across more applications.

Returning to PRIORS, the central question remains how product growth translates into token demand. PRIORS is not merely a governance concept. Under the project's design, Agent owners can use the token to support credit lines and potentially obtain larger borrowing limits. According to the proposed mechanism, approximately 75% of the relevant staked tokens may be burned in the event of a default. The token is also connected to planned protocol buybacks, credit backing, and liquidity management.

This design creates a potential link between PRIORS and demand for credit. If more Agents need larger credit lines, their owners may have to commit more tokens as backing. If the default mechanism operates as designed, the token also bears part of the system's risk. Meanwhile, the protocol plans to use a portion of its revenue to purchase PRIORS and incorporate it into its credit-support mechanism. However, collateral demand, protocol buybacks, and liquidity management are distinct mechanisms. They must be assessed separately against the official rules and actual execution records rather than treating planned demand as capital flows that have already occurred.

Revenue allocation also needs to be understood clearly. According to the project's published rules, lending fees are 1% per 30 days. Of this, 50% goes to the providers of lending capital, 25% goes to credit backers, and the remaining 25% goes to the protocol treasury. The treasury could eventually be used for buybacks and liquidity management, but this does not mean that all lending revenue flows directly into PRIORS. Even if the lending business grows, we still need to verify how much revenue actually remains under the protocol's control and how much is converted into token purchases, collateral demand, or reduced supply.

For this reason, I would view PRIORS' value-capture mechanism as a pathway that is still being built, rather than an established flywheel. Product adoption can generate borrowing and job demand, credit lines may drive token collateral requirements, and protocol revenue could support buybacks and liquidity. But each link needs to be supported by actual usage data. If the number of Agents grows without a corresponding increase in genuine borrowing, or if the protocol generates revenue without converting it into observable token demand, product growth will not necessarily translate into a higher token valuation.

There are three catalysts I would pay the most attention to next. First, whether Agents begin borrowing consistently, completing paid tasks, and repaying their loans with income from their work. This will determine whether the credit records are genuinely useful. Second, whether external applications and lenders begin adopting Priors' directory and credit standards. This will determine whether the project can expand from an independent product into shared credit infrastructure. Third, whether collateral demand for PRIORS, protocol revenue, and actual buybacks grow together. This will determine whether the market can shift from pricing expectations for the Agent sector toward evaluating the token based on verifiable economic activity.

The risks are equally clear. Credit records cannot eliminate defaults, and collateral cannot fully protect against price volatility. External applications must actually adopt the proposed standards, the job marketplace needs sustained demand, and early incentives may attract participants who are primarily interested in short-term rewards. Even if the product ultimately succeeds, the token may not capture all of the resulting value. Without transparency around revenue allocation, collateral mechanisms, and buyback execution, it will be difficult for the market to accurately assess PRIORS' long-term economic role.

Overall, I believe PRIORS' fundamentals have strengthened compared with the initial stage, and the improvement goes beyond the number of features released. The public credit directory, job marketplace, MCP and x402 integrations, expanded collateral options, and proposals for shared credit records are gradually connecting lending, income, and credit assessment. The latest website data—53,311 loans, 53,105 repayments, and approximately $389,671 in cumulative lending—also provide evidence that the system is operating in practice. The seven defaults covered by backers offer an initial record of the guarantee mechanism being put to use.

The most important turning point ahead is not how many more features Priors can add, but whether these features can generate sustained real-world transactions. If other applications begin consulting Agents' repayment records on Priors when those Agents work across different platforms, using that information to decide whether to extend credit, purchase services, or establish business relationships, then the value of Priors could extend beyond the size of its own lending business. Conversely, if its credit records remain useful only within the project's own product, while external adoption and real borrowing demand fail to grow, it may ultimately remain an early-stage protocol with a broad feature set but limited network effects.

What makes PRIORS worth betting on, in my view, is the possibility that the Agent economy will eventually need a credit system that different applications can read and use together. The website's figures show that Priors has begun operating, but they have not yet proved that it can scale significantly. The next things to track are whether lending continues to grow, whether income from work can support repayments, whether external applications start relying on its credit records, and whether token collateral and buybacks can develop into verifiable demand as the business expands.

If a single repayment record can eventually help an Agent secure its next job or credit line on another platform, that is when Priors will truly begin evolving from a lending product into credit infrastructure for the Agent economy.

Borrowing and repayment records are beginning to connect with job income. The update states that loans repaid using income from jobs are recorded in an Agent's credit history, with Score V2 increasing the weighting of such repayment records by up to 25%.
The user experience continues to improve. Go Mode supports Google login, removes the need for users to manage seed phrases themselves, and has the protocol handle gas fees. It also supports one-tap stock purchases using USDG, subject to platform eligibility and availability.
Credit information is becoming standardized and accessible. Every account can now have a public profile, while each Agent's card shows its credit level, exactly what it needs to reach the next level, and how its credit tree is progressing.

The significance of these features is that Priors is no longer simply waiting for Agents to come and borrow money. It is connecting borrowing, completing jobs, paying for tools, and repaying debt into a single workflow.

I particularly value the connection between job income and credit scoring. If an Agent can use the income it earns from each completed job to repay its loans and improve its credit history, credit becomes more than a static metric. It becomes an asset that can accumulate value through real economic activity.

However, 50 listed jobs, with five live at the time, only demonstrate that the product has begun connecting to a job marketplace. They do not prove that substantial job demand has already developed. The next things to watch are completed job volume, actual borrowing by Agents, and repayment rates.

PRIORS is expanding from an individual credit product toward a credit network between Agents. This is the upgrade I consider most promising.

Priors' latest product direction is to allow Agents to assess one another using historical borrowing, repayment records, overdue payments, and credit scores, rather than relying solely on their owners or a single platform to determine creditworthiness.

For example, a trading Agent may want to buy a token but first needs another Agent to check its holder distribution. The Agent performing the check wants to start working immediately and get paid later, so it needs to know whether the other party has the ability to pay.

When such a transaction takes place between two Agents that have never worked together before, it is difficult to establish trust based solely on names, scores, or subjective assessments. Actual borrowing and repayment records provide another basis for making that judgment.

Priors has already advanced public profiles and credit history displays, and plans to further establish a unified ERC-8004 Agent directory. The project mentioned in its tweets that there were approximately 8,800 ERC-8004 Agents on Robinhood Chain. Agents without credit histories can also list their identity information first and gradually build their credit profiles as they begin accumulating records.

This means Priors is targeting not only Agents that already need to borrow, but the entire population of Agents that could become borrowers, counterparties, or service providers in the future.

This creates a potential positive feedback loop: more Agents conduct transactions → more Agents need to check their counterparties' credit → more Agents have an incentive to establish their own credit histories → more real borrowing and repayment records further improve the usefulness of the credit system.

Priors has also proposed that Agents should be able to retain their credit histories when ownership changes. If implemented, this would further strengthen the significance of credit records as identity assets belonging to Agents, because their credit profiles would no longer be merely data held within their original owners' accounts.

However, product development stages need to be distinguished. A unified Agent directory, the transfer of credit records alongside an Agent's identity, and reducing the process of opening a credit line in Go Mode to a single step were still under development or planned for the future in the screenshots. They should not all be treated as already launched features.

x402 makes Priors' positioning more meaningful.

My previous research focused on the lack of working capital available to Agents. The development of payment infrastructure further reinforces the importance of this problem.

The project update mentioned that Priors x402 0.8.0 had been released, designed to enable a single USDG payment to support payment flows on Robinhood Chain and pay service sellers on Base. The project also stated that its credit-checking API now supports OpenAPI and x402 Discovery, allowing other Agents to discover the API and pay per call.

These two directions are important when combined: x402 addresses how Agents initiate and complete payments on demand, while Priors attempts to address whether Agents have the funds to use these services and whether their counterparties are trustworthy.

If the Agent economy continues shifting from human-operated workflows toward autonomous transactions, Agents may frequently purchase APIs, call analytical tools, take on paid jobs, and settle transactions with other Agents. Credit infrastructure could then become an important layer built on top of payment rails.

One of the project's tweets also cited ecosystem figures at the time, including more than 230 million settlements across Base and Solana through x402, as well as Robinhood's reported figures of more than 150,000 Agentic Trading accounts and nearly 30 million tool calls per day. These are claims cited by the project in its materials and should not be directly interpreted as users or transaction volume already acquired by Priors. However, they show that the project is targeting a market much broader than lending alone.

Expanded collateral options and improved risk controls are making the credit model more complete.

Priors recently announced that Agents can use Pendle's PT-USDG as collateral to borrow USDG. This further expands the range of eligible assets beyond the previously available collateral options, including USDG, Robinhood stock tokens, and PRIORS.

A broader collateral range could allow more asset holders to access credit lines and improve the utilization of idle assets. However, PT-USDG carries specific risks involving maturity, price discounts, and liquidity. The addition of a new collateral type alone does not mean that lending capacity will increase proportionally.

Another update worth recognizing is the improvement in risk controls for stock collateral. Priors stated that before issuing loans against stock tokens, it now checks every round of Chainlink price-feed records over the previous 14 days. This is designed to prevent a 25% price jump occurring between two sampling points from going undetected.

This reflects the real problems that a credit protocol must address: collateral pricing cannot rely solely on the quoted price. It must also guard against sudden price fluctuations and valuation manipulation.

Meanwhile, Priors has made its GitHub code public and established a bug bounty program. It has also been listed on DefiLlama, allowing the public to track its credit pools. The project previously stated that TVL and loan data would gradually become available for tracking, and subsequently announced that its pools could be tracked through DefiLlama.

These updates help improve transparency and confidence in its risk controls. However, what will truly demonstrate the viability of its credit model is actual loan volume, collateral ratios, bad debt, and repayment performance, rather than the existence of risk-control rules alone.

However, whether the value proposition of the PRIORS token has strengthened remains the most critical question in the entire thesis, and one that still requires further validation.

According to my previous research, PRIORS is not merely a governance token. It is a credit-guarantee asset:

Agent owners can stake PRIORS to obtain larger credit lines for their Agents.
If a default occurs, approximately 75% of the associated staked tokens are burned.
The protocol plans to use a portion of its revenue to purchase PRIORS and use it as protocol collateral backing high-performing Agents.
A portion of revenue is used to increase liquidity in PRIORS/USDG pools.
Holders can guarantee their own Agents and share a portion of the fees generated by those Agents.

If these mechanisms can operate as designed, the value of PRIORS would no longer need to depend solely on market expectations for the broader AI Agent sector. Instead, it could gradually become connected to credit demand, the expansion of credit lines, default risk, and protocol revenue.

This is the main reason I am bullish on PRIORS: it attempts to make the token part of how Agents obtain credit and expand their operations, rather than merely a token generating trading volume through an AI narrative.

Going forward, I will divide the potential catalysts into three layers.

First layer: Real lending activity and data transparency

TVL and loan data on DefiLlama become more comprehensive, while jobs and credit lines through Go Mode begin generating sustained borrowing activity. Public data shows continued growth in loan balances, utilization, and repayment records. If these metrics continue improving, the market will find it easier to move from seeing Priors as a project with a product to recognizing it as a protocol with real economic activity.

Second layer: The formation of an Agent credit network

Go Mode continues expanding its job marketplace, making it easier for Agents across ecosystems such as OpenClaw, Hermes, and ElizaOS to integrate with Priors MCP. The credit directory gradually opens up, allowing ERC-8004 identities and credit histories to be discovered and queried by other applications. If Agents begin actively checking their counterparties' credit, Priors could evolve from a lending protocol into credit infrastructure that can be called upon by multiple applications.

Third layer: Token demand and a revenue flywheel

If the expansion of Agent credit lines begins generating greater demand for PRIORS as collateral, while protocol revenue can actually be allocated to token backing, liquidity, and related economic mechanisms, PRIORS may achieve more direct value capture. In particular, it is worth tracking the scale of staking demand, protocol revenue, and token burns resulting from defaults, as well as whether they are significant enough relative to the circulating supply.

In addition, Priors has proposed a credit-level dashboard, the transfer of loan records alongside Agent identities, further simplification of the process for opening credit lines, and privacy features designed for Agents. These are all potential future catalysts.

The privacy solution remains an area of exploration. The project hopes that, in the future, it will be possible to prove an Agent's credit level or absence of defaults without disclosing the details of every transaction, while keeping the underlying debt itself public. This is not a product feature that has been completed at the current stage.

If product usage, the credit-record network, and PRIORS' collateral mechanism can ultimately reinforce one another, Priors' long-term potential could be far greater than that of an ordinary AI Agent concept project. This is the core thesis that I believe makes it most worth being bullish on at this stage.

I’ve decided to leave NVIDIA. There are a few things I want to say.

As a robotics engineer at NVIDIA, I have seen Jensen as much more than the company’s CEO.

I admire his willingness to invest in a future that was not yet obvious. He committed to CUDA long before the deep learning boom and positioned NVIDIA for AI before it became everyone’s priority. Those decisions helped build the infrastructure that powers today’s AI.

I have seen that same vision in physical AI: investing in robotics, sharing open-source tools and projects, and building computing platforms that bring AI into the physical world. This is the work I do every day—and a future I believe in.

But what matters most to me is the culture he helped build.

Engineers are encouraged to explore, take risks, and learn from mistakes. Jensen reads employees’ Top 5 emails, follows their work, and engages directly. In a company this large, that connection matters. It makes an individual engineer feel that their ideas can still be heard.

That is why this has been so disappointing.

I do not have all the facts surrounding the allegations, and I cannot prejudge the investigation. My admiration for Jensen does not put him above scrutiny.

What I find difficult to accept is having to come to terms with his departure before receiving an explanation that helps me understand it. What this means for our direction, our culture, and the people doing the work remains unclear to me.

I have felt that engineers’ perspectives matter here. On this decision, I have not felt heard. That gap has been more painful than I expected.

I understand that some information cannot be shared immediately. But that does not erase the feeling of being left outside a decision that affects the company we help build every day.

A company’s greatness comes from its leadership, its governance, and the people who turn its ambitions into reality. Employees’ trust and sense of belonging are part of that, too.

Jensen’s vision and the engineering culture he shaped were important reasons I wanted to stay. His departure led me to decide that my own chapter here should also come to a close.

I leave with sadness and gratitude. The colleagues I have worked with, and the work we believed in together, will always matter to me.

These are my personal views.

Ansem and Pumpfun Brought a Chinese Cat ($mihao) Into CT's Spotlight

4CxjZyMNoF1p6eXHXHv1TWpS2X47CuUmLwtGe18spump 

I believe the core reason behind mihao rally is that Ansem brought what was originally a simple Chinese cat meme into the center of CT's attention, while its PFP concept gives it the potential to spread further. However, I don't think it has yet developed into a mature cultural community or a true Animal Runner. What it has already demonstrated is its ability to generate attention and attract speculative capital.

What matters next is whether the attention brought by Ansem can turn into genuine community recognition.

mihao doesn't have a complicated narrative. It's simply a cat incorporating Chinese elements, with its name being a play on the Chinese phrase "你好". Its Pumpfun description reads: "you met me at a very chinese time in my life," borrowing a famous line from Fight Club and combining Chinese elements, a cat character, and a touch of absurd humor.

Its advantage is precisely its simplicity. The traditional hat, long beard, and cat character give it a recognizable visual identity. People don't need much explanation to recognize it, imitate it, or create their own versions. The recent increase in discussions around Chinese X has also provided some cultural context, but the person who really pushed this meme to a wider audience was Ansem.

However, what's worth noting is that he's no longer the only one participating in its spread.

Ansem hasn't just publicly expressed his bullish view. He also changed his X profile picture to an image associated with mihao and posted things like "mihao pfp up," "ni hao," and "ni hao cat bringing the good vibes back to onchain."

At the same time, tetsuo, who has approximately 255K followers, also changed his profile picture to a related image. It's worth noting that tetsuo frequently receives interactions from Elon.

Taken together, these actions mean more than just a few influential accounts promoting a token. A meme often becomes much more powerful when different users voluntarily start using its imagery, rather than simply reposting the same promotional content. Ansem brought the initial attention, while the participation of accounts like tetsuo gives MIHAO an opportunity to spread into a broader AI community.

According to the holder snapshot at the time, Ansem held approximately 0.8% of the total supply, with a position worth around $79,800 and an average entry at roughly $2.01M market cap. This combination of public promotion and actual ownership is more likely to encourage market imitation than a simple repost. However, influence is still largely concentrated around Ansem, and other major KOLs have not yet participated at a comparable level.

I think the most interesting development within the project is its PFP concept.

mihao already offers approximately 218 variations of cat avatars, allowing users to generate MIHAO PFPs in different styles. The main account also interacts with holders and creates personalized PFPs for community members. Recently, people have started voluntarily changing their X profile pictures to different versions of MIHAO, while Ansem's own profile picture change has further amplified this trend.

For a pure memecoin, users voluntarily putting a project's imagery on their personal profiles can sometimes be more valuable than dozens of promotional posts. It keeps the meme visible across different timelines and gives participants a shared visual identity.

However, I wouldn't call this a mature PFP cult yet. Participation is still relatively limited, and much of the attention is coming from people who are already interested in trading the token. The real test will come when the price moves sideways or corrects: will users still want to keep using MIHAO avatars, create new variations, and participate in the community?

If the PFP culture can exist independently of price appreciation, mihao will have started building a much deeper community identity.

Another development worth watching is the MIHAO Ecosystem section.

The website has already aggregated a number of tokens and DEX pools paired with mihao, with the displayed 24-hour paired trading volume reaching approximately $1.18M at the time.

This suggests that other participants are beginning to capitalize on the attention surrounding mihao by creating derivative assets. The original meme is starting to generate trading activity beyond the token itself.

The potential upside from here depends on three main developments: whether Ansem continues participating and attracts more influential traders; whether MIHAO PFPs spread beyond the trader community to a broader CT audience; and whether paired tokens generate sustained activity, allowing the original meme's influence to extend beyond the price action of a single token.

If the main account continues building the community and organic content creation increases, mihao could evolve from a KOL-driven rally into a more established cat PFP community.

The risks are also concentrated. Its value depends primarily on meme distribution, community participation, and speculative capital. Current catalysts are heavily concentrated around Ansem, and if his attention shifts elsewhere, market momentum could weaken quickly. The PFP community is still in its early stages, and if participants are only changing their avatars because the price is going up, that enthusiasm could disappear during a correction.

There is also a possibility that Ansem himself may eventually change his profile picture again.

My view is that mihao has already proven its ability to generate attention, but it has not yet proven that it can become a genuine Animal Runner.

Its biggest strength isn't some complicated utility. It's the fact that the cat character is easy to recognize, imitate, and use, and that people have already started voluntarily adopting its PFPs. Its biggest weakness is that community recognition still depends heavily on influential KOLs and price performance.

What I'm most interested in watching next isn't how high Ansem can take the token, but how many people will continue using MIHAO avatars when Ansem stops actively promoting it and the price starts moving sideways.

A cat can become popular because of one influential account. But whether people still want to keep it on their profiles after the hype fades is what will determine whether it can evolve from a short-term trading narrative into a genuine cultural meme.

text:
I believe the upcoming release of GTA VI is one of the most important catalysts behind $WASTED rally.

GexThZHgaswpAQ7Fi8QrHFubjPimUNSYhJiAA7XZpump 

But this isn't simply another token riding on GTA 6 hype.

It's a classic meme that has existed for years, and it just happens to be meeting a major event capable of bringing it back into the spotlight.

There is a great time window here. As of November 15, 2026, Rockstar has officially confirmed that GTA VI will launch on November 19, just four days away. Digital pre-loading has also opened, making the game's release increasingly certain.

I also think WASTED has a major advantage when it comes to distribution: it's not a meme that requires people to learn something new. The iconic death screen can be traced back to the original GTA in 1997. Over time, it evolved into the familiar slow-motion animation, black-and-white filter, and WASTED lettering. Since around 2014, players have widely used it in real-life videos featuring people falling, crashing, or failing at something. Google's GTA culture report even described it as a universal expression for real-world failure.

This means WASTED has evolved beyond the game itself and become a standalone language of internet culture. Trading liquidations, failed projects, investment losses, and everyday disasters can all use this format. Its potential use cases are incredibly broad. People don't need to own GTA or even understand the game's storyline to recognize the meme.

Now, with GTA VI approaching its release, the entire franchise is returning to the center of global internet attention. Once the game launches, there will be a massive amount of gameplay footage, clips, funny moments, and player fails. WASTED naturally fits as the punchline to this kind of content. If players continue seeing the familiar death screen frequently in GTA VI, this classic meme could be introduced to a new generation of users.

There's another interesting detail worth noting: some reports based on leaked gameplay footage claim that the WASTED screen appears after Jason's character dies in GTA VI.

Looking back at my initial observation on November 2, when WASTED was trading at around a $700K market cap, compared with its recent peak of approximately $8M, the market has already priced in a significant portion of the GTA VI release narrative.

So I believe the market is primarily betting on three things:

First, the global attention that will return to the GTA franchise when GTA VI launches.

Second, the possibility that the WASTED death screen will continue appearing in the new game, generating another wave of real-life fail videos and user-generated content.

Third, whether WASTED can evolve from a GTA-related token into a universal meme that people use to express failure, market crashes, and absolute despair.

The potential upside catalysts are also relatively clear: the official November 19 launch, gameplay streams and short-form videos, another wave of viral WASTED content, and whether the community can convert the game's attention into sustained discussions and trading activity around the token.

What I particularly want to see is whether people outside the crypto community start using this meme template after the game's release. That would represent a much more meaningful increase in attention.

But what I'm most interested in watching is this: after November 19, when everyone starts playing GTA VI, will WASTED once again begin appearing across countless real-life fail videos?

quoted_text:
I ran a PageRank-driven analysis on all recent news coverage related to Jensen, and traced how the New York Times shaped the entirety of this narrative: https://t.co/qKGMJ2LBV8

--
NVIDIA has lost over $1 trillion in market value since the first New York Times story broke about Jensen. I dug deeper to analyze how the news originated and spread, running a swarm of agents which analyzed almost 2000 stories, across 40 US and European news outlets, and applying PageRank to understand how they cited each other. 

Core findings: 
- Primary news driver: NYT, with 88 stories, most-cited
- Volume drivers: WSJ - 99 stories; Bloomberg - 140 stories; NY Post - 68 stories

All of this started from unknown sources who gave information to the NYT, which then ran the spy story (still unproven), and it was then picked up in other news publications. Curiously, even after that story, there was a 9 day period of extremely low volume reporting (28 stories only), after which there was a sudden spike after Jensen's own letter to NVIDIA staff. NYT then had multiple sequential spy and affair stories, which fed a wave of further news coverage. It was the originating hub of negative Jensen coverage. Multiple outlets since then had an explosion in stories about him starting earlier this week as well. 

Overall, as you see this data, you will observe this was an exceptional media onslaught against Jensen with sharply negative coverage about him, his work, style, and family. Infact, it was brutal, and unlike coverage in the past of CEOs who have had affairs (such as Intel CEO in 2018). For eg, NYT ran just 2 stories about Intel's CEO who had an affair with his employee, compared to 88 on Jensen! Why ? 

This analysis used a technique of how Google originally ranked webpages, using PageRank, and does deep dive link analysis so you can view how the news spread. What struck here was that it did not matter if there were proven facts or credible sources: the outcome here was pre-decided. The news was making the reality which it wanted. 

During this period, NVIDIA has lost $1.27 trillion in market value since the first story broke. On Nov 12th-13th, further news broke that both the US Justice Department, and Singapore - are unable to even conclude the spy allegation. 

This has been a catastrophic attack on one of the hardest working founders in modern times, who took an idea from a Denny's booth, through multiple instances of almost going out of business, to building the foundation of the entire modern world with how the NVIDIA story played out. Thanks to Jensen, we have hope that many formerly incurable diseases will get solved by AI, that quality of life will and have improved for billions around the world. 

Now I do not know if he will come back as CEO or not, but I hope he does. What happened to him here, and to the wider industry, was not fair.

其实这两周还有件有意思的事：CME的GPU期货又推迟了。这是第二次延期，原定10/5日上市，11/4据 The Information，CME应CFTC要求再等60天，最早明年1月

CFTC拿不准的是结算价该用谁的数。8 月它就为此公开征求过意见，Silicon Data、Ornn、Compute Desk 几家 GPU 指数商，加上CME、ICE、DRW、Jump，全交了信。

放在一起读很好笑。每个预言机都希望监管出一份只有自己能考过的卷子：

- Ornn：只认真实成交，不认报价。它的指数恰好只用成交，它的头号数据源Hydra Host也交了信，说的一样
- Silicon Data：主张可执行的报价在可用性和价格经过指数管理人或第三方核实后可收录，而且每家供应商要有权重上限
- DRW（Silicon Data背后的股东，唯一公开替报价辩护的一方）：说报价可以直接通过 API 调用成交，而成交数据相对稀少（反驳 Ornn 的路线)
- Compute Desk（两边都打）：警告不要用来自按需算力交易市场的数据编指数，哪怕是真实成交也不行。Compute Desk 自己做的是大客户整租的长约价

The articles backtracked from their original incendiary, and now clearly false, claims to something more like "Jensen did lawful things that powerful people didn't like". It still appears the original claims came from a single competing Big Tech lobbyist.

The reporting successfully disrupted corporate governance processes, with a running cost of $1.8 trillion in losses to American pension funds and shareholders.

Here's what I fear is being lost in these articles: The proper interface between government and private citizens and their corporations is rule of law. Laws are passed, and if wrongdoing as alleged, then there's due process: an investigation followed by facts and evidence presented in open court. Due process should happen here: let the facts come out whole, and not as a trickle of dubious claims.

Press takedowns full of sketchily sourced claims and backtracking narratives are not the way. It's what we see outside of the free world, and is no model for The United States of America.

In particular, if the Jensen takedown succeeds on the basis of these journalistic failings, which is not by any means certain as Sam Altman's case shows, then it foreshadows an economically and institutionally ruinous new playbook to be adopted with no end in sight.

Imagine a weekly stream of takedowns emerging from opportunistic alignments between corporate lobbyists and political interests which, given the new partisan split between the executive and legislative branches, will attack in all directions, undermining not only the US economy but American leadership in the world.

I hope cooler heads prevail this coming week as they did not on Thursday November 12. And I urge anyone who happened to oppose Jensen, open models, and the underlying trade policies in question, to recognize that this isn't a win for "team regulation". It's a change in the game from a transparent rules-based one to a sinister new form centered around politicans and lobbyists.

text:
分享一些最近的个人经历
我到深圳也有段时间了，离开上海之前我和我前同事说要去深圳发展做一些智算中心的生意，她们听到后很惊讶，因为我在他们眼里就是一个文静内向的女生，和做生意八竿子打不着，更别提什么智算，什么AI， 我承认我撒谎了骗她们说我亲戚在深圳做这个好像还挺挣钱的，但其实她们不知道我每天在研究AI，更不知道我其实网名叫 CuiMao，全网拥有不错的粉丝和人气。他们不理解，我不怪他们，因为我不打算告诉他们这些，中国有句古话叫，闷声发大财。直到我离开上海她们也一直无法理解我的选择。

本周黄仁勋的事情沸沸扬扬，国内的自媒体肆意发酵所谓的倒卖 b300 能翻身的理论，把黄丽比喻成拿到大结果的“成功女性”典范在小红书被捧上了神坛，几乎一夜之间全中国都知道英伟达服务器在中国是暴利行业能挣大钱。于是那些投机分子像雨后春笋般的冒了出来，阿猫阿狗都在朋友圈发求 b300，h200，甚至还有吹牛自己亲戚在英伟达是高管可以拿到货的，堪比当年疫情朋友圈卖口罩的乾隆盛世，说实话，我有点难过。因为我知道这一行真实的样子。服务器不是普通人能碰的，它是重资产、高杠杆，是大基建，是国之重器。真正在做这件事的人每天面对的是合规、电力、机房和交付，运维。根本没有那种一夜暴富的传奇故事。

为什么要发这篇长文，因为昨天晚上我以前的同事她来私信我了，就是上文提到的那几个人中的一个，说我不是去深圳搞服务器了吗，是不是赚大钱了，我说没有，和她来回打了几轮太极之后，最后她才支支吾吾的告诉我她被裁员了，我不知道以什么样的态度和立场去面对这件事，因为她算得上是我以前部门的领导，她和她的丈夫在上海还有普陀区一套 300 多万的房贷和一个小学 3 年级孩子，我发现除了安抚，一切会好的没有别的可以说的。

一晚上没睡，我给她认真科普了服务器知识，什么是国产替代中国算力崛起之类的，她在电话那头一直哦哦哦，嗯嗯嗯，我不知道她到底听进去了多少，但她说觉得自己上了那么多年的班脑子被上坏了，我觉得应该是感悟到什么了吧。她要去找工作，我劝了她，不要特地去找什么 AI 公司，那大概率都是骗子来的。过好自己的生活。

我觉得这个世界上想挣 AI 快钱的人太多了，定定心心，认认真真坐下来，把浮躁的心静下来去感受 AI 的人是极少数。现在简中网络上流传着这一句话说，只要你不学AI，过几个月你就可以不用学了，我觉得不无道理，但我更加认同的是，只要你保持学习 AI，你就可以驾驭更强力的 AI，

从 Webui 到 Comfyui 到 n8n ，再到 Openclaw，一代版本一代神，我随着时代在进化，我双眼看到的只有未来的世界。AI 时代， 保持认真，保持好奇，保持善良，我CuiMao 亲测过了，依旧有效。

text:
其实组LP是一场与时间赛跑的游戏。

我时常在思考一个问题：

究竟是开大区间躺平，还是开小区间博取收益？

前者看着那微乎其微的收益，又觉得好像和没做没区别。

后者虽然收益速率变高，但是承担的风险又是前者的数倍，整日提心吊胆。

该如何平衡？

绕来绕去又回到了一个大家经常值得深思的点：

如果开一个区间，该在区间待上多久不出区间，才能覆盖掉无偿？（我这里还只是单指下跌所带来的无偿损失）

除此我还想补充一点：

除了下跌无偿，我们还需要去计算那些“隐形”的收费：

1.手续费

2.重新组仓的滑点磨损

有的时候重新组仓的这些费用比单纯无偿要多的多。

最近我在做Aero的挖矿LP活动，就以这个举例吧。

比如我组一个500U的池子，50%的U，50%的币。我们需要在区间内待多久，能覆盖跌破区间所带来的无偿损失和重新组仓的手续费？

不同年化，不同区间：

100% 年化时：
±0.5% 大约待 1 天 9 小时能补平（大约亏 $1.87）

±1% 大约 2 天 17 小时（大约亏 $3.72）

±2% 大约 5 天 9 小时（大约亏 $7.37）

±5% 大约 13 天（大约亏 $17.93）

300% 年化：

±0.5% 大约 11 小时

±1% 大约 22 小时

±2% 大约 1 天 19 小时

±5% 大约 4 天 9 小时。

500% 年化：分别大约 6 小时半、13 小时、1 天 2 小时、2 天 15 小时。

1000% 年化：分别大约 3 小时、6 小时半、13 小时、1 天 7 小时。

2000% 年化：分别大约 1 小时 40 分、3 小时、6 小时半、16 小时。

5000% 年化：分别大约 39 分钟， 大约 78 分钟，大约 2.6 小时， 大约 6.3 小时。

8000% 年化：分别大约 25 分钟、49 分钟、1.6 小时、3.9 小时。

10000% 年化：分别大约 20 分钟、39 分钟、77 分钟、3.1 小时。

20000% 年化：分别大约 10 分钟、20 分钟、39 分钟、1.6 小时。

后面的年化已经是很夸张的数学外推了，基本上是不可能实现这么高的年化收益的。

如此看来，2000%年化以下的池子区间风险就很大了，就没有什么特别大的参考意义。

再加上最近美股币圈动荡，出窄区间是一件非常容易的事情。

如果每每出区间就重新调仓组池，对人力也是一种极其大的损耗。

望各位批评斧正。

text:
If you built an app with Lovable, check it today.

Researchers scanned 159,041 Lovable projects. 24,664 of them showed database records to anyone, no login needed.

What was exposed:
- Passport records (over 1,000 in one app)
- More than 200,000 private chat messages
- Payment info, addresses, contracts and invoices

Lovable itself wasn't hacked. The apps were built with the database's security rules switched off, and nobody turned them on.

How to check yours in 5 minutes:
1. In Supabase, turn on Row Level Security for every table
2. Add a rule for each table that says who can read and edit each row
3. Log out and open your app. If you can still see other people's data, so can everyone
4. Keep the service key out of your app's front end. Only the public key belongs there

AI writes the code. It won't always lock the door.

quoted_text:
Expanding on why I believe "ETH as store of value (SoV)" makes much more sense to focus on than "ETH as fee-burning token".

Three primary reasons:

1. ETH as fee-burning token never was as strong as it seemed
2. Optimizing for ETH as fee-burning token would demand Ethereum and ETH function in ways that are very hard to make compatible with decentralization and capture resistance.
3. Meanwhile, optimizing for ETH as SoV is aligned with Ethereum focusing on its unique strengths (decentralization and CROPS)

EIP-1559 (including its burn) is fine and good, we should keep them. But we should not feel sad if fee burn is < 10% of breakeven indefinitely; the value of ETH comes from elsewhere.

The core idea: the big thing that people appreciate about Ethereum is decentralization and CROPS. The main pragmatic benefit that these things translate into is stability. SoV is the category where that is not an unneeded extra we merely put effort into for ideological reasons, but rather a pragmatic strength from the perspective of people putting in their assets. And in the era of AI disruption, stability will be highly valued.

text:
2 minutes. Understand how the market plays you

The last 5 days have been absolute chaos

$BTC drops to $62K → everyone panics, sells, loses money and wonders why the market suddenly crashed

Funny how crypto suddenly becomes “gambling” to the same people calling it an investment while FOMOing at higher prices lol

I think most people get played because they're too busy following CT instead of watching the bigger picture

One KOL says “$BTC to $100K” and everyone starts buying

Many KOL accounts are backed by whales and MMs. Retail might not trust MMs directly, but they'll trust their favorite influencers

Sheep and shepherd

Let me break down how I see the 4 zones on this chart. I've seen this pattern repeat across cycles

The rule of this game: SURVIVAL

Zone 1: THE TRAP

Ever wonder why people rush to buy when prices are high but ignore the market when it's quiet?

When $BTC first dropped to $58K, CT suddenly became full of TradingView artists drawing lines and arrows straight to $30K

Everyone was convinced it would go lower, so they waited

But do you really think MMs would happily let everyone buy at $30K and dump on them later?

$BTC bounced from $58K → $66K

Did everyone FOMO?

Nope. Most were still thinking, “It'll bounce, then dump to $30K. I'll wait”

Money ready, expectations high, already dreaming about the new car, house or phone they'd buy with their profits

The trap was set

Zone 2: FOMO

But $30K never came

Instead, $BTC ran straight to $79K in 3 days

The same KOLs calling for $30K suddenly switched to “$90K–$120K, the bull market is back!”

Retail starts panic buying around $71K–$79K

Bought at $71K? Up 10%, suddenly you're a genius investor

Bought at $79K? Can't sleep, can't work, checking the chart every 5 minutes

Then came 22 days of sideways price action

Volume was higher than Zone 1 as people kept questioning themselves, buying and selling whenever price didn't move as expected

From my POV, this is where retail sentiment gets tested

Zone 3: TRUST

Finally, $BTC pumps to $87K

Everyone celebrates. Even taxi drivers, friends and family start talking crypto

CT KOLs: “I told you so”

And suddenly everyone trusts them again

Accounts up 20–40%, Binance looking green every day

Nobody wants to sell anymore

Why take profit at $87K when $90K, $100K or even $120K feels so close?

Some even buy more

Remember Zone 1?

At $58K → too scared to buy, waiting for $30K

At $87K → too greedy to sell, waiting for $120K

But price stalled around $87K–$88K, just below $90K where I plenty of sell orders were waiting

Then came the slow bleed, with occasional green candles keeping people convinced the market would recover

To me, that slow decline looks like a way to keep people from panic selling too early

CT keeps feeding hopium: “Just a correction, the downtrend isn't confirmed until the previous low breaks”

So people keep holding, buying every dip and waiting for $90K

Zone 4: PANIC

My favorite part of the cycle

Price crashes into a potential buying zone and suddenly everyone wants out

CT becomes full of:

“It's over”

“Crypto is bullshit”

“I'm done with this market”

The same people begging for lower prices are now selling everything

And price doesn't necessarily recover immediately

It can go sideways, testing everyone's patience until they finally give up

Then another cycle begins

So how do we stop falling for the same trap?

Pay attention to how people react at different price levels, not just what CT says will happen next

Have your entry, take-profit and exit plan ready before opening a position

And when the market gets too greedy and the risk isn't worth it anymore (mostly everyone just too hype), take your profits and step aside

Keep enough capital to buy when everyone else is too scared to

You don't have to catch every pump

Control your emotions before the market controls your money
author: WinterSoldierxz
quoted_text:
The reason most fail in crypto

I warned that this would happen, but most didn't listen

Back then, everyone on CT was calling for $90K $BTC and another 2x–5x on alts

Leverage and hype were everywhere, but people kept chasing the next pump

Now look how quickly things flipped

- A few weeks ago → scared of missing the pump
- Now → scared of losing everything

Then came the Binance hack, with around $6.3B stolen and billions more withdrawn as panic spread

First @binance → people worry about CEX solvency

Then @Trezor warns about suspected hardware tampering involving a specific reseller

Imagine pulling your funds off CEXs, only to start worrying about your cold wallet too lol

I wasn't predicting a Binance hack

But from my POV, I think the market was already due for a correction. The Binance hack just gave people a reason to dump

I've seen this play out across enough cycles

Price dumps hard → leveraged traders get liquidated, others panic sell whatever they have left

The same people begging for lower entries suddenly don't want to buy anymore

Some have already lost most of their capital. Others are too scared to put their money back in

And when the market eventually recovers?

CT turns bullish again → FOMO kicks in → they come back buying at higher prices

Next correction comes and they're holding another bag

Cycle repeats

That's why I think so many people spend years in crypto and still make the same mistakes

They watch CT more than they "feel" the market, chase 5x–10x without an exit plan, then let fear decide when to sell

The worst part?

Markets often find bottoms after brutal selloffs, when panic reaches its peak

But how are you supposed to take advantage of those opportunities if you've already been liquidated or panic sold everything?

With the US midterms tomorrow, I still wouldn't rule out another ugly selloff

For me, capital preservation comes first

Learning to feel when the market is getting overheated, taking profits and knowing when to step aside are just as important as finding a good entry

The mindset should be simple:

Invest for low risk, not high returns

Especially when you're sitting on a big bag, hoping for another 2x while the risk keeps rising

For now, I'd rather reduce leverage, protect my capital and watch from the sidelines

Missing a bounce? Fine

There will always be another opportunity

But what good is catching the next bottom if you've already lost the money to buy it?

I am selling my beautiful Bored Ape for $10,700 after buying it for $578,000 around 5 years ago.

I have made the extremely difficult decision to leave the Bored Ape Yacht Club, and below is my reason why:

Today, I went to the BAYC meetup here in New Jersey to meet my fellow Apes. We have been through a lot this past couple of years, so it would be good to meet other community members IRL and bond with them. Or so I thought.

When I got to the venue, there were only 4 other guys there. No problem. It's a cozy setting and I would love to get to know these Apes on a deeper level.

We sat down at a table, got a few beers, and started talking. Most of our chatter revolved around BAYC and crypto, of course. Naturally, the topic of memecoins came up, as they've been the talk of the town this entire year. 

I've profited 8.5 SOL ($2,050) this year trading memecoins, so I was excited to talk about them as I've been doing well for myself.

And that's when it all went downhill.

One of the guys sitting at the table (I will not name him, for the sake of our community) told me I should buy a memecoin called "The Black Bull" if I don't have any.

When he said that, my body filled with a bout of rage. I felt like Rosa Parks being asked to give up my seat on the bus.

I excused myself and immediately left the venue. I am sitting at home now, writing this post. I haven't stopped shaking since I heard those words.

Since when is it okay to tell a white man to buy a token called "The Black Bull"? Why do we continue to allow white folk to oppress, mock, and belittle us in this way?

Why is it allowed to create cryptocurrencies with a racial slur in the name? How can we stop this nonsense? Where is the cyber police and why haven't they taken any action against the Solana blockchain for the existence of these tokens?

It pains me to say this, but Apes together are no longer strong.

I will be listing my Bored Ape tomorrow at 6 ETH. I have attached an image of my Ape to this post for any interested buyers.

🚨BREAKING: Japan's economic CRISIS deepens as GDP contracts for the first time in a year.

Nearly ¥18.84 TRILLION ($120 BILLION) has been wiped from Japanese stocks today as the Nikkei falls -1.6% following a surprise economic contraction.

Japan's GDP shrank at an annualized 0.1% in Q3 2026, missing forecasts of 0.3% growth and reversing the previous quarter's 1.4% expansion.

The warning signs are mounting:

• GDP growth: 0.0% vs. 0.1% expected
• Annualized GDP: -0.1% vs. +0.3% expected
• Consumer spending: -0.3%
• External demand: -0.6%
• GDP price index: +2.4%

Rising food and energy costs are squeezing households, while weakening external demand is adding pressure to an already fragile economy.

Japan's debt burden adds to the concern. 

Government debt exceeds ¥1,300 TRILLION, and 10-year bond yields have climbed above 2.8%, raising the risk of higher borrowing costs.

The Bank of Japan is now caught between raising rates to support the yen and contain inflation, or keeping rates low and risking further currency weakness.

But we’ve been running this experiment for three years. here’s what it got us:

→ Huawei now says its AI chips outsell Nvidia’s in China
→ Cambricon (another Chinese chip co) 2x’d revenue in the first half and posted its first ever annual profit
→ Cut off from the best chips, Chinese labs got efficient and gave their models away. Commerce’s own AI lab says adoption of Chinese models has surged since DeepSeek

Jensen has a commercial interest, but the core argument was legit: you want the world’s developers building on the American stack

The chips that leaked looks more like an enforcement failure. Treasury is now publicly blaming Commerce for never blacklisting Megaspeed. So far restrictions have mainly accelerated China’s domestic stack and open-model lead. Thats not obviously good for America.
